RISKS IN RELATION TO THE FIRST OFFER 
This being the first public issue of Equity Shares of our Company, there has been no formal market for the Equity Shares of o ur Company. The face value of the 
Equity Shares is ₹10 each. The Floor Price, Cap Price and the Offer Price as determined by our Company, in consultation with  the book running lead managers 
(“BRLMs”), on the basis of the assessment of market demand for the Equity Shares by way of the book building process, in accordance with the SEBI ICDR 
Regulations, and as stated in “Basis for Offer Price” beginning on page 158 should not be considered to be indicative of the market price of the Equity Shares after 
the Equity Shares are listed. No assurance can be given regarding an active and/or sustained trading in the Equity Shares nor regarding the price at which the Equity 
Shares will be traded after listing. 
GENERAL RISK

* Our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs, may consider participation by Anchor Investors in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations. The Anchor 
Investor Bid/ Offer Period shall be one Working Day prior to the Bid/ Offer Opening Date. 
** Our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs and in accordance with the Offer Agreement, may consider closing the Bid/ Offer Period for QIBs one Working 
Day prior to the Bid/ Offer Closing Date in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations. 
***  The UPI mandate end time and date shall be at 5:00 p.m. on the Bid/Offer Closing Date. 
^  Our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs, may consider a  Pre-IPO Placement ( as defined below) of  specified securities, as may be permitted under 
applicable law, at its discretion, aggregating up to ₹900.00 million, in one or more tranches prior to filing of the Red Herring Prospectus with the RoC. The Pre-
IPO Placement, if undertaken, will be at a price to be decided by our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs. If the Pre -IPO Placement is completed, the 
amount raised pursuant to the Pre -IPO Placement will be reduced from the Fresh Issue, subject to compliance with Rule 19(2)(b) of the SCRR. The Pre -IPO 
Placement, if undertaken, shall not exceed 20% of the size of the Fresh Issue. The utilisation of these proceeds raised pursuant to the Pre-IPO Placement will be 
done towards the proposed objects of the Offer in compliance with applicable law. Prior to the completion of the Offer, our Company shall appropriately intimate 
the subscribers to the Pre-IPO Placement, prior to allotment pursuant to the Pre-IPO Placement, that there is no guarantee that our Company may proceed with 
the Offer or the Offer may be successful and will result into listing of the Equity Shares on the Stock Exchanges. Further, relevant disclosures in relation to such 
intimation to the subscribers to the Pre-IPO Placement (if undertaken) shall be appropriately made in the relevant sections of the Red Herring Prospectus and 
the Prospectus, and details of the Pre-IPO Placement, if any, shall be reported to the Stock Exchanges within 24 hours of such transactions, in accordance with 
Regulation 54 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations.  
Investments in equity and equity-related securities involve a degree of risk and Bidders should not invest any funds in the Offer unless they can afford to take the 
risk of losing their entire investment. Bidders are advised to read the risk factors carefully before taking an investment decision in the Offer. For taking an investment 
decision, Bidders must rely on their own examination of our Company and the Offer, including the risks involved. The Equity Shares in the Offer have neither been 
recommended, nor approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“ SEBI”), nor does SEBI guarantee the accuracy or adequacy of the contents of this 
Draft Red Herring Prospectus. Specific attention of the Bidders is invited to “Risk Factors” beginning on page 26.

confirmed by or relating to our Company, any other Selling Shareholder or any other person(s) in this Draft Red Herring Prospectus. 
LISTING 
The Equity Shares of face value of ₹10 each, that will be offered through the Red Herring Prospectus are proposed to be listed on the stock exchanges being, BSE 
Limited (“BSE”) and National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE” and together with BSE, the “Stock Exchanges”). For the purposes of the Offer, [●] shall

change on the respective websites of the BRLMs and at the terminals of the Syndicate Members and by intimation to Self-Certified Syndicate Banks (“SCSBs”), the Designated Intermediaries and the Sponsor Banks, as applicable. 
This Offer is being made in terms of Rule 19(2)(b) of the SCRR read with Regulation 31 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. The Offer is being made through the Book Building Process and is in compliance with Regulation 6(2) of the SEBI ICDR

Portion”) provided that our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs, may allocate up to 60% of the QIB Portion to Anchor Investors on a discretionary basis in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations (“Anchor Investor Portion”), of 
which 40% of such Anchor Investor Portion shall be reserved in the following manner  (i) 33.33% shall be reserved for allocation to domestic Mutual Funds ; and (ii) 6.67% shall be reserved for Life Insurance Companies and Pension Funds , 
subject to valid Bids being received from domestic Mutual Funds , Life Insurance Companies and Pension Funds at or above the Anchor Investor Allocation Price. In the event of under-subscription in (ii) above, the allocation may be made to 
domestic Mutual Funds, at or above the price at which Equity Shares will be allocated to the Anchor Investors (“Anchor Investor Allocation Price”), in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations. In the event of under-subscription or non-
allocation in the Anchor Investor Po rtion, the balance Equity Shares shall be added to the QIB Portion (excluding the Anchor Investor Portion)  (“Net QIB Portion”). Further, 5% of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a 
proportionate basis only to Mutual Funds and the remainder of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a prop ortionate basis to all QIB Bidders (other than Anchor Investors) including Mutual Funds, subject to valid Bids being 
received at or above the Offer Price. If at least 75% of the Net Offer cannot be Allotted to QIBs, then the entire Bid Amount will be refunded forthwith. However, if the aggregate demand from Mutual Funds is less than 5% of the Net QIB 
Portion, the balance Equity Shares available for allocation in the Mutual Fund Portion will be added to the remaining Net QIB Portion for proportionate allocation to QIBs. Further, not more than 15% of the Net Offer shall be available for 
allocation to Non-Institutional Bidders (“Non-Institutional Bidders” or “NIBs”) wherein (a) one-third of such portion shall be reserved for NIBs with application size of more than ₹0.20 million and up to ₹1.00 million; and (b) two-third of such 
portion shall be reserved for NIBs with application size of more than ₹1.00 million, provided that the unsubscribed portion in either of such sub-categories may be allocated to NIBs in the other sub-category (“Non Institutional Portion”) and 
not more than 10% of the Net Offer shall be available for allocation to Retail Individual Bidders (“Retail Individual Bidders” or “RIBs”) in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations (“Retail Portion”), subject to valid Bids being received 
from them at or above the Offer Price. Further, Equity Shares will be allocated on a proportionate basis to Eligible Employees Bidding under the Employee Reservatio n Portion, subject to valid Bids being received from them at or above the 
Offer Price (net of Employee Discount, if any). All potential Bidders (except Anchor Investors) are required to mandatorily participate in the Offer through the Application Supported by Blocked Amount (“ASBA”) process by providing details

• changes in marketplace policies, commission structures, sponsored listing costs, advertising bidding models, data privacy

• unfavorable customer reviews, ratings or social media commentary, including in relation to product quality, delivery

Further, according to the Redseer Report, the Indian next generation consumer appliances sector is characterized by intensifying 
competition, supply-side dependencies, and execution complexities, which may impact the ability of technology-led players to 
sustain growth, maintain differentiation, and achieve profitable scale. Certain threats and challe nges in the sector are set out 
below (based on the Redseer Report): 
 
• Intensifying competition and technology diffusion may reduce differentiation and pricing power:  The sector is 
witnessing heightened competition from established multinational and domestic players with strong brand equity, extensive 
distribution, and scale advantages, alongside emerging digital -first brands leveraging asset -light models, competitive 
pricing, and online channels. As adoption of energy-efficient technologies, including BLDC motors and electronic control 
systems, continues to expand, companies may need to sustain product innovation, brand positioning, and channel execution 
to maintain differentiation and command premium pricing over time. This may result in pricing pressures, higher customer 
acquisition costs, and an increasing emphasis on brand strength, innovation, and distribution reach as key competitive 
differentiators 
 
• Dependence on imported electronic components exposes supply chain, cost, and currency risks:  Increasing 
electronics content has led to continued reliance on imported components such as semiconductors and controllers, exposing 
companies to global supply disruptions, geopolitical developments, and foreign exchange fluctuations. Variability in 
component availability and pricing may impact production planning and cost structures. While localization efforts are 
progressing, limited domestic availability of high-value components may continue to pose near- to medium-term challenges 
 
• Volatility in raw material prices may impact cost structures and margins:  The industry remains sensitive to 
fluctuations in key raw materials such as steel, copper, aluminium, and plastics, driven by global commodity cycles and 
macroeconomic conditions. Changes in input costs may affect manufacturing expenses and margins, parti cularly where 
cost pass-through is constrained. Sustained volatility may require ongoing cost optimization and sourcing efficiency  
 
• Execution complexities in scaling omnichannel distribution and manufacturing operations: Expansion across offline 
retail, e -commerce, and direct -to-consumer channels introduces operational complexity. Offline growth requires 
investments in distribution, inventory, and working capital, while digital channels face rising customer acquisition co sts. 
Scaling manufacturing involves challenges in capacity ramp -up, process standardization, and maintaining product quality 
at higher volumes. Inefficiencies may impact unit economics, margins, and customer experience

• Consumer price sensitivity and evolving demand patterns may moderate adoption of premium products:  While 
demand for energy-efficient and performance-led appliances is increasing, a significant portion of the market remains price-
sensitive, particularly in mass segments. Higher upfront costs may limit broader adoption. Evolving preferences toward 
smart and connected appliances require continuous innovation and accurate demand forecasting. Misalignment with 
consumer adoption or slower uptake in certain categories may impact growth and returns. 
 
Any increase in competition, including from global players, domestic incumbents or new entrants, may result in pricing pressure, 
loss of market share, increased marketing and distribution costs, and reduced margins. Our ability to compete effectively als o 
depends on our ability to maintain strong relationships with distributors and retailers, sustain our online channel leadership, and 
deliver consistent product quality and after -sales service. Any failure to do so may adversely affect our brand, customer 
acquisition and retention. 
 
Accordingly, any inability to compete effectively on price, quality, innovation, brand positioning or distribution may adversely 
affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

75. Our business may be adversely affected by adverse application or interpretation of competition laws in India.  
 
The Competition Act, 2002, as amended (the “Competition Act”) was enacted for the purpose of preventing practices that have 
or are likely to have an adverse effect on competition (“AAEC”) in certain markets in India and has mandated the Competition 
Commission of India (the “ CCI”) to prevent such practices. Under the Competition Act, any arrangement, understanding or 
action, whether formal or informal, which causes or is likely to cause an AAEC is deemed void and attracts substantial penalties. 
 
Further, any agreement among competitors which directly or indirectly involves determination of purchase or sale prices, limits 
or controls production, or shares the market by way of geographical area or number of consumers in the relevant market is 
presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition in the relevant market in India and shall be void. Further, the 
Competition Act prohibits abuse of dominant position by any enterprise. If it is proved that the contravention committed by a  
company to ok place with the consent or connivance or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, 
secretary or other officer of such company, that person shall be guilty of the contravention and liable to be punished.  
 
The Competition Act aims to, among others, prohibit all agreements and transactions which may have an AAEC in India. 
Consequently, certain agreements entered into by us could be within the purview of the Competition Act. Further, the CCI has 
extra-territorial powers and can investigate any agreements, abusive conduct or combination occurring outside India if such 
agreement, conduct or combination has an AAEC in India. The effects of the provisions of the Competition Act on the 
agreements entered into by us cannot be predicted with certainty at this stage. However, we may be affected, directly or 
indirectly, by the application or interpretation of any provision of the Competition Act, any enforcement proceedings initiat ed 
by the CCI, any adverse publicity tha t may be generated due to scrutiny or prosecution by the CCI, or any prohibition or 
substantial penalties levied under the Competition Act, which would adversely affect our business, results of operations, cas h 
flows and prospects. 
 
The Government of India has also passed the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, which has proposed several amendments 
to the Competition Act, such as introduction of deal value thresholds for assessing whether a merger or acquisition qualifies  as 
a “combination”, expedited merger review timelines, codification of the lowest standard of “control” and enhanced penalties for 
providing false information or a failure to provide material information. It also reduces the overall time limit for the assessment 
of combinations by the CCI from 210 days to 150 days and empowers the CCI to impose penalties based on the global turnover 
of entities, for anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position, among others.  
 
If we pursue acquisitions in the future, we may be affected, directly or indirectly, by the application or interpretation of any

81. Investors may have difficulties enforcing foreign judgments against us or our management.  
 
Our Company is a company incorporated under the laws of India. All of our Directors are citizens and residents of India. A 
substantial portion of our Company’s assets are located in India. As a result, it may be difficult for investors to effect service of 
process upon us or such persons in India or to enforce judgments obtained against us or such parties outside India.  
 
Recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments is provided for under Section 13 and Section 44A of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908, as amended (the “ Civil Procedure Code ”). India is not a party to any international treaty in relation to the 
recognition or enforcement of foreign judgments. India has reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and 
commercial matters with a limited number of jurisdictions, i ncluding the United Kingdom, Singapore, UAE, and Hong Kong. 
A judgment from certain specified courts located in a jurisdiction with reciprocity must meet certain requirements of the Civ il 
Procedure Code. The United States has not been notified as a recipro cating territory. 
 
In order to be enforceable, a judgment obtained in a jurisdiction which India recognizes as a reciprocating territory must me et 
certain requirements of the Civil Procedure Code. Section 13 of the Civil Procedure Code provides that foreign judgments shall 
be conclusive regarding any matter directly adjudicated on except (i) where the judgment has not been pronounced by a court 
of competent jurisdiction, (ii) where the judgment has not been given on the merits of the case, (iii) where it appears on the face 
of the proceedings that the judgment is founded on an incorrect view of international law or refusal to recognize the law of India 
in cases to which such law is applicable, (iv) where the proceedings in which the judgment was obtained were opposed to natural 
justice, (v) where the judgment has been obtained by fraud or (vi) where the judgment sustains a claim founded on a breach of  
any law then in force in India. Under the Civil Procedure Code, a court in India shall, on the production of any document 
purporting to be a certified copy of a foreign judgment, presume that the judgment was pronounced by a court of competent 
jurisdiction, unless the contrary appears on record; such presumption may be displaced by proving want of jurisdiction. The 
Civil Procedure Code only permits the enforcement of monetary decrees, not being in the nature of any amounts payable in 
respect of taxes, or other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalty and does not provide for the enforcement 
of arbitration awards even if such awards are enforceable as a decree or judgment. A foreign judgment rendered by a superior 
court (as defined under the Civil Procedure Code) in any jurisdiction outside India which the Government of India has by 
notification declared to be a reciprocating territory, may be enforced in India by proceedings in execution as if the judgment had 
been rendered by a competent court in India. Judgments or decrees from jurisdictions which do not have reciprocal recognition  
with India cannot be enfor ced by proceedings in execution in India. Therefore, a final judgment for the payment of money 
rendered by any court in a non -reciprocating territory for civil liability, whether or not predicated solely upon the general laws 
of the non -reciprocating terri tory, would not be enforceable in India. Even if an investor obtained a judgment in such a 
jurisdiction against us, our officers or directors, it may be required to institute a new proceeding in India and obtain a de cree 
from an Indian court. 
 
However, the party in whose favor such final judgment is rendered may bring a new suit in a competent court in India based on 
a final judgment that has been obtained in the United States or other such jurisdiction within three years of obtaining such final 
judgment. It is unlikely that an Indian court would award damages on the same basis as a foreign court if an action is brought in 
India. Moreover, it is unlikely that an Indian court would award damages to the extent awarded in a final judgment rendered 
outside India if it believes that the amount of damages awarded were excessive or inconsistent with public policy in India. In  
addition, any person seeking to enforce a foreign judgment in India is required to obtain the prior approval of the RBI to repatriate 
any amount recovered, and we cannot assure that such approval will be forthcoming within a reasonable period of time, or at

all, or that conditions of such approvals would be acceptable. Such amount may also be subject to income tax in accordance 
with applicable law. Further, any judgment in a foreign currency would be converted into Indian Rupees on the date of judgment 
(and not on the date of payment), which could also increase risks relating to foreign exchange.  
 
Consequently, it may not be possible to enforce in an Indian court any judgment obtained in a foreign court, or effect service of 
process outside of India, against Indian companies, entities, their directors and executive officers and any other parties re sident 
in India. Additionally, there is no assurance that a suit brought in an Indian court in relation to a foreign judgment will b e 
disposed of in a timely manner.

2. Brand awareness and performance marketing activities 
 
Our Company proposes to utilize an amount of up to ₹1,500.00 million from the Net Proceeds towards the brand awareness 
and performance marketing activities of our Company. Marketing and advertising are integral to our Company’s growth 
strategy as they ensure that our Company’s products and services are known to our target audience; our target audience 
being the AB1 urban consumers (as identified by the new consumer classification system under the Indian Socio -
Economic Classification framework), and that our Company’s offerings do not go unnoticed. Further, targeted advertising

(i) Aris Contour – Focus of the R&D effort behind the Aris Contour was placed on aerodynamic performance, with an 
aerofoil narrow blade design developed to achieve efficient air delivery; the blade design was extensively simulated 
to optimise the choice of aerofoil geometry and twist angles along the length of the blade, with the in -house testing 
facility leveraged to conduct air delivery, noise, vibration, thermal, and reliability tests. Further, with the introduction 
of moonbeam interface in Aris Contour, the moonbeam interface has been adopted as the standard interface adopted 
across our subsequent and upcoming models. 
 
(ii) Emperion Linea – Central to R&D behind Emperion Linea was the introduction of a metal extruded blade, developed 
to achieve a differentiated design aesthetic. Acoustics formed a key engineering objective, with the product 
engineered to be the most silent fan in the portf olio. Given the complexity introduced by the combination of 
integrated LEDs and a compact motor, thermal management of electronics was addressed through a combination of 
simulation and testing, ensuring reliable performance within the constra ined physical architecture of the product.

(iii) Intellon – The development of the Intellon, our water purifier, was driven by an assessment of the residential water 
purifier category, conducted through market surveys, consumer interactions, and industry expert engagements, which 
identified significant consumer f riction points including elevated total cost of ownership, limited transparency on 
product performance, and structural dependency on recurring service contracts. R&D activities undertaken for the 
Intellon led to the development of a water flow arc hitecture with strategic sensor placement that provides an 
additional degree of freedom for water movement to the drain, enabling features such as accurate filter life estimation, 
Vacay mode, and TDS creep reduction. Further, dedicated in-house test facilities of more than 3,000 square feet were 
established to test the reliability of electrical components, sensor calibration, and individual and system -level filter 
life, supplemented by third -party laboratory testing. Fine -tuned algorithms were also develope d to enable features 
such as TasteTune and Vacay mode. Collectively, these R&D activities underpin a connected service model designed 
to reduce reliance on the annual maintenance contracts.

development-led (R&D) company that (i) builds next-generation consumer appliances; and (ii) designs, manufactures 
and supplies proprietary and critical components to enterprise customers, with applications across different industries. 
As an outcome of our sustained investments across technology, product innovation, manufacturing integration and 
omni-channel distribution, according to the Re dseer Report, we are the only scaled consumer appliances company in 
India that combines (i) proprietary motor and electronics design developed in -house, (ii) integrated manufacturing of 
critical differentiating components, (iii) a digital -first omni -channel distribution model, and (iv) an enterprise 
components business built on the same underlying technology platform.  
 
Listed consumer appliance companies in India typically outsource critical component manufacturing, significantly 
under-invest in R&D and rely on traditional distribution models. Accordingly, it is not possible to provide an industry

ANNEXURE “1” TO THE STATEMENT OF SPECIAL TAX BENEFITS AVAILABLE TO THE COMPANY AND 
ITS SHAREHOLDERS UNDER THE APPLICABLE TAX LAWS IN INDIA  
 
Outlined below are the special tax benefits available to the Company and its shareholders under the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the 
Act’) as amended by the Finance Act, 2026 and Income-tax Rules, 1962 , along with circulars and notifications issued thereon 
i.e., applicable for the Financial Year (‘FY’) 2025-26 relevant to the Assessment  Year (‘AY’) 2026-27, and the Income Tax 
Act, 2025 as amended by the Finance Act, 2026 and Income-tax Rules, 2026 i.e. applicable for Tax Year 2026-27 (collectively 
hereafter referred to as the “Direct Tax Laws”) presently  in  force  in India, as per the Direct Tax Laws.     
 
A. Special tax benefits available to the Company under the Act     
 
1. Lower corporate tax rate 
 
Section 115BAA was inserted by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 (“the Amendment Act, 2019”) w.e.f. April 1, 
2020 (AY 2020-2021) granting an option to domestic companies to compute corporate tax at a reduced rate of 25.17% (22% 
plus surcharge of 10% and cess of 4%), provided such companies do not avail specified exemptions/incentives (e.g. deduction 
under Section 10AA, 32(1)(iia), 33ABA, 35(2AB), 80-IA etc.).  
 
        The Amendment Act, 2019 further provides that domestic companies availing such option will not be required to pay Minimum 
Alternate Tax (“MAT”) under Section 115JB. The CBDT has further issued Circular 29/2019 dated October 02, 2019 clarifying 
that since the MAT provisions under Section 115JB itself would not apply where a domestic company exercises option of lower 
tax rate under Section 115BAA, MAT credit would not be available. Corresponding amendment has been inserted under Section 
115JAA dealing with MAT credit. 
 
Further, Income-tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and section 115BAA of the erstwhile Income-
tax Act, 1961 has been replaced by a similar section 200 under the Income -tax Act, 2025 and  section 115JB of the erstwhile 
Income-tax Act, 1961 has been replaced by a similar section 206 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. 
 
The Company has opted for concessional rate under section 115BAA of the IT Act from FY 2019-20 onwards. From AY 2020-
21 to AY 2026 -27, the Company has followed Section 115BAA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and from Tax Year 2026 -27 
onwards, the Company shall follow Section 200 of the Income Tax Act, 2025. 
 
2. Deductions from Gross Total Income in respect of employment of new employees  
 
Subject to fulfilment of prescribed conditions, the Company is entitled to claim deduction, under the provisions of Section 
80JJAA of the Act, of an amount  equal to 30% of additional employee cost (relating to specified category of employees) 
incurred in the course of business in the previous year, for three assessment years including the assessment year relevant to the 
previous year in which such employment is provided.   
 
The deduction under section 80JJAA of the Act is available even if the Company opts for concessional tax rate under section 
115BAA of the Act, subject to fulfilment of conditions laid  
down under the provisions of section 80JJAA of the Act. 
 
Further, Income-tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and section 80JJAA of the erstwhile Income -
tax Act, 1961 has been replaced by a similar section 146 under the Income -tax Act, 2025. 
 
3. Deduction in respect of inter-corporate dividends 
 
A new Section 80M has been inserted by the Finance Act, 2020 w.e.f. April 1, 2021 providing for deduction from gross total 
income of a domestic company, of an amount equal to dividends received by such company from another domestic company 
or a foreign com pany or a business trust as does not exceed the amount of dividend distributed by it on or before one month 
prior to the date of filing its tax return as prescribed under Section 139(1) of the Act.  
 
Where the Company receives any such dividend during a FY and also, distributes dividend to its shareholders before the 
aforesaid date, as may be relevant to the said FY, it shall be entitled to the deduction under Section 80M of the Act.  
 
Further, Income-tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and section 80M of the erstwhile Income -tax 
Act, 1961 has been replaced by a similar section 148 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. 
 
4. Foreign tax credit (‘FTC’)  
 
Provisions of double taxation relief and FTC in India are governed by Sections 90 and 91 under Chapter IX - 'Double Taxation 
Relief of the Act read with Rule 128 of Income Tax Rules, 1962.

169 
Section 90/ section 91 of the Act provides that where a resident taxpayer who has suffered double taxation in respect of his 
income is eligible to avail relief of taxes paid in foreign country in accordance with the aforementioned provisions provided  
under the Act. 
 
Further, Income-tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and Sections 90 and 91 of the erstwhile Income-
tax Act, 1961 has been replaced by similar Sections 159 and 160 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Simultaneously, Income Tax 
Rules, 2026 has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and Rule 128 of the erstwhile Income -tax Rules, 1962 has been 
replaced by similar Rule 76 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. 
 
5. Deduction in respect of specified expenditure (Public issue expenses)  
 
As per Section 35D (1)(ii) of the Act, expenditure incurred by the Company post commencement of business, in connection 
with extension of undertaking or setting up of a new unit shall be allowed as deduction @ 1/5th of expenditure for five 
successive years  beginning with the previous year in which the extension of the undertaking is completed or the new unit 
commences production or operation.  
 
Subject to the fulfilment of above conditions prescribed under Section 35D of the Act, the Company may be eligible to claim 
amortised deduction in respect of specified preliminary expenditure, including expenditure incurred in connection with the issue 
of shares to the public depending upon the nature of the expenditure, its nexus with the public issue, and the purpose for which 
the proceeds of the public issue are ultimately utilised. 
 
Further, Income-tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and Section 35D of the erstwhile Income -tax 
Act, 1961 has been replaced by a similar Section 44 under the Income-tax Act, 2025.  
 
6. Capital gains taxation 
 
As per Section 112 of the IT Act, where the total income of the assessee includes any income, arising from the transfer of a 
long-term capital asset, which is chargeable under the head ‘Capital gains’, the tax payable on the same shall be chargeable at 
the rate of 12.5% (plus applicable surcharge and health and education cess). 
 
As per section 112A of the Act, long -term capital gains arising from transfer of listed equity share, or a unit of an equity -
oriented fund or a unit of business trust shall be taxed at the rate of 12.5% (without indexation) of such capital gains wher e the 
transfer takes place on or after July 23, 2024. It is worthwhile to note that tax shall be levied where such capital gains ex ceed 
INR 125,000. 
 
As per section 111A of the Act, short term capital gains arising from transfer of a listed equity share, or a unit of an equi ty-
oriented fund or a unit of a business trust shall be taxed at 20% of such capital gains subject to fulfilment of prescribed conditions 
under the Act. 
 
Further, Income -tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and Sections 112, 112A and 111A of the 
erstwhile Income -tax Act, 1961 has been replaced by similar Sections 197, 198 and 196 under the Income -tax Act, 2025 
respectively. 
 
B. Special tax benefits available to Shareholders    
 
1. Dividend income earned by the shareholders would be taxable in their hands at the applicable rates. However, in case of 
domestic corporate shareholders, deduction under Section 80M of the Act would be available on fulfilling the prescribed 
conditions.  Further, in case of shareholders who are individuals, Hindu Undivided Family, Association of Persons, Body 
of Individuals, whether incorporated or not, surcharge would be restricted to 15%, irrespective of the amount of dividend 
income. 
 
Further, Income-tax Act, 2025, has been enacted with effect from April 1, 2026, and section 80M of the erstwhile Income -tax 
Act, 1961 has been replaced by a similar section 148 under the Income-tax Act, 2025.

Deep-tech engineering platforms are redefining India's consumer appliances market  
 
Deep-tech engineering platforms are driving a structural shift in India’s consumer appliances market. These companies are built 
on proprietary, research & development driven technologies across core engineering domains such as materials & chemistry, 
energy and power systems, intelligence, sensing, and connectivity, supported by integrated and flexible manufacturing 
capabilities for critical components and industrial design. Together, these capabilities enable scalable deployment across 
product categories, d elivering sustained improvements in performance, efficiency, and reliability while creating durable and 
difficult-to-replicate competitive advantages. Consumer appliances are at an inflection point, with deep -tech engineering 
platforms driving the adoption of next-generation consumer appliances in India. Structural tailwinds including rising incomes, 
increasing digital adoption, regulatory tightening, supportive policy initiatives like Make in India and a growing focus on 
resource efficiency are further acc elerating adoption of next -generation consumer appliances, with India still underpenetrated 
relative to global markets, indicating significant headroom for growth.  
 
Deep-tech engineering platforms are built on proprietary technology modules that generate durable competitive 
advantages across multiple applications 
 
Deep-tech engineering platforms refer to businesses that: (i) incur research and development expenditure of at least 5% of 
revenue from operations; (ii) have at least 25% of their workforce engaged in dedicated research and development and 
engineering functions; and (iii) develop products across multiple categories based on a common engineering and technology 
platform comprising proprietary, internally developed technologies embedded within the core product architecture and 
manufacturing processes. These technologies span domains including materials and chemistry, energy and power systems, and 
intelligence, sensing and connectivity, enabling measurable improvements in product performance, efficiency, and reliability.  
Sustained investment across these domains  provides control over critical elements of the product architecture, including 
component technologies, manufacturing processes, and product design, enabling the reuse of core technologies across multiple 
products and consumer appliance categories, while facilitating rapid innovation, scalable production, and adaptation to evolving 
consumer requirements. As these capabilities mature, they can be leveraged across adjacent categories and industrial 
applications, driving the transition from a product-led model to a technology-led platform. 
 
Deep-tech engineering platforms are characterised by three defining attributes:  
 
• Sustained research & development investment directed at core component technologies: Research & development 
efforts are focused on the continuous evolution of foundational technologies, strengthening the underlying technology base 
and expanding its applicability across use cases. With each development cycle, technical capabilities deepen a nd control 
over critical elements of the product architecture increases. As a result, deep -tech engineering platforms advance further 
along the technology maturity curve, while assembly -led players increasingly converge toward established industry 
standards. 
 
• Proprietary capability across five foundational technology domains : Companies build and retain capabilities across 
these core technology domains, each representing a distinct source of competitive differentiation. These are embedded at 
the component level, enabling performance advantages and raising barriers to entry ove r time.

180 
o Materials and chemistry:  Critical materials are engineered through proprietary formulations and developed in close 
collaboration with specialized vendors, rather than sourced as standard inputs, enabling superior characteristics such 
as conductivity, strength, and thermal resistance.  
 
o Energy and power systems:  Differentiation is driven by integrated systems that manage how energy is converted, 
regulated, and delivered. These are designed alongside physical components, enabling improved efficiency, thermal 
management, and operational stability 
 
o Intelligence, sensing and connectivity: Smart embedded electronics use real-time operating data such as temperature, 
current, and speed to optimize performance, enable fault detection, and support predictive maintenance. A connectivity 
layer comprising IoT hardware, applications, and cloud infrastructure further enables remote monitoring, smart home 
integration, and data -driven personalization, enhancing user experience while supporting continuous product 
improvement post-deployment. 
 
o Proprietary process and manufacturing:  Specialized manufacturing processes that are deeply embedded within the 
production architecture, represent a more durable barrier to entry than product -level intellectual property. Unlike 
component or industrial design that can be reverse -engineered or lic ensed, proprietary process know -how is 
accumulated through successive production cycles and is difficult to replicate. This includes tightly controlled 
production environments, precision tooling, and process -specific expertise that are critical determinants of product 
performance, consistency, and yield.  
 
o Industrial design language:  Proprietary architecture removes the form -factor constraints imposed by commodity 
components, enabling two distinct advantages. Functionally, product layouts can be optimized for greater space 
efficiency, higher functional integration, and improved perform ance. Aesthetically, it enables a consistent industrial 
design language, creating a visually distinct and premium product identity.  
 
• Integrated manufacturing architecture: Deep-tech engineering platforms develop flexible manufacturing architectures 
aligned with product design, enabling common sub-assemblies and standardized interfaces to be deployed across multiple 
products and variants. This improves manufacturing efficienc y and supports scalable production from a common 
technology base. The scalability of these platforms is further strengthened by integrated supplier ecosystems capable of 
supporting specialized components and manufacturing requirements. Over time, close supplier collaboration builds process 
familiarity and engineering alignment, supporting faster product development, improved cost efficiency, and consistent 
component quality.  
 
The extensibility of deep -tech engineering platforms allows proprietary technologies to be deployed across multiple growth 
pathways. Within consumer markets, foundational technologies developed in core product categories can be leveraged across 
adjacent applications with limited incremental engineering effort, enabling efficient portfolio expansion and broader utilization 
of research & development investments. As these technologies mature, they can also be commercialized through proprietary 
components and s ub-systems supplied to OEMs and industrial customers. Together, expansion across consumer applications 
and OEM value chains enables deep -tech engineering platforms to leverage technology investments across a wider set of 
products, applications, and end markets.

appliances such as washing machines, refrigerators, and televisions. Across each of these categories, appliances built on

conventional mechanical designs cannot deliver.  
 
Next-generation consumer appliances refer to products built on higher efficiency, technology -led architectures that deliver 
superior performance compared to conventional mechanical systems. These appliances integrate electronics and embedded 
software with components such as digitally controlled motors, sensors, intelligent power management systems, and design -led 
product architectures, enabling more precise regulation of operation, intuitive user interaction, and stable performance acro ss 
varying usage cond itions. Integrated control over technology and product design further enables optimized internal layouts, 
higher functional integration, and a differentiated industrial design language characteri sed by sleek interfaces, minimalistic 
form factors, and high-technology aesthetics aligned with evolving consumer preferences. 
 
A subset of these appliances further extends these capabilities through connectivity features such as app -based control, usage 
tracking, and diagnostic alerts, enabling greater transparency, remote access, and enhanced user control. Next-generation 
appliances increasingly layer software driven user experience on top of hardware performance, with connectivity, intuitive user 
interfaces, and data -driven reporting collectively driving higher engagement and more personalized usage. Together, these 
technology-led designs translate into three measurable consumer benefits, including lower lifetime energy costs through 
improved efficiency, more consistent performance under real world conditions, and enhanced user experience

• Motor technology: Appliances have evolved from basic DC brushed, AC induction, and AC universal motors with limited 
control and lower efficiency arising from frictional, copper, and slip-related losses, toward advanced ECM (“Electronically 
Commutated Motors”) and inverter -based systems. Advancements across m otor control, magnetic architecture, topology, 
and material science have enabled precise speed and torque control, lower energy losses, and improved operating 
performance. Technologies such as FOC (“Field Oriented Control”) have significantly enhanced effi ciency, smoothness, 
and responsiveness during operation, while continued advancements in radial and axial flux motor topologies, premium

• Power electronics: Historically, appliances used electromechanical or analog power regulation (mechanical regulators, 
resistive circuits), leading to energy losses and limited dynamic control. Advances in semiconductor switching devices and 
embedded control systems have enabled the transition to modern power electronics architectures. The adoption of solid -
state components such as Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistors (“MOSFET”s) and Insulated-Gate Bipolar 
Transistors (“IGBT”s) allows electrical energy to be regu lated through high -frequency switching rather than resistive 
dissipation. This enables dynamic modulation of power delivery based on operating demand, supporting variable -speed 
operation, improved energy efficiency, and more stable and responsive appliance  performance 
 
• Software capabilities: Software capability in next -generation appliances spans both embedded device intelligence and 
connected consumer experience layers. At the device level, proprietary firmware continuously enhances appliance 
performance, diagnostics, efficiency, and reliabi lity through real -time optimization and adaptive control. At the 
connectivity layer, integrated IoT stacks, cloud infrastructure, dedicated application ecosystems, and AI/ML -driven 
personalization capabilities are transforming appliances from standalone products into adaptive, connected systems. These 
capabilities enable remote monitoring and control, automation, usage analytics, predictive diagnostics, OTA updates, 
continuous data feedback loops, and ongoing optimization within broade r connected home ecosystems 
 
• Control systems: Traditionally, appliances relied on mechanical switches, timers, and basic analog circuitry, limiting their 
ability to dynamically optimize performance across varying operating conditions. Advances in embedded electronics have 
enabled the adoption of micr ocontrollers, sensor -based feedback systems, and software -driven control algorithms that 
facilitate precise, real -time control of speed, power, temperature, and operating cycles. Modern control systems 
increasingly incorporate proprietary firmware and adva nced motor control architectures such as FOC, enabling higher 
operating stability, responsiveness, energy efficiency, and reliability, while supporting seamless integration between 
hardware, embedded intelligence, and software layers

Regulatory standards and policy initiatives are accelerating the transition towards efficient, locally manufactured consumer 
appliances in India 
 
Regulatory push is accelerating the shift toward next -generation, energy -efficient appliances while strengthening domestic 
supply chains in India. Key regulatory and policy initiatives supporting this transition include:  
 
• Bureau of Energy Efficiency (“BEE”) star labelling scheme and Minimum Energy Performance Standards 
(“MEPS”): These frameworks provide transparent benchmarks for appliance efficiency, enabling consumers to compare 
products based on electricity consumption. Efficiency standards have become progressively more stringent over time, 
raising baseline performance requirements and improving the lifecycle cost competitiveness of next-generation appliances. 
As a result, manufacturers are increasingly adopting newer technologies to meet evolving benchmarks, accelerating the 
penetration of solutions such as BLDC motors in ceiling fans. Similar regulatory tightening across other categories has also 
driven meaningful efficiency gains, with the Ministry of Power noting that successive revisions to BEE star -rating norms 
have improved the energy efficiency of entry-level split air conditioners by approximately 43%. 
 
• Production Linked Incentive (“PLI”) scheme for white goods: The scheme aims to strengthen domestic manufacturing 
capabilities and reduce import dependence in critical appliance components such as motors, compressors, Printed Circuit 
Boards (“PCBs”), and control electronics. As of January 2025, 84 companies have bee n approved under the scheme with 
committed investments of approximately ₹104.78 billion (approximately US$ 1.2 Billion), supporting the development of 
domestic manufacturing capacity for these key  components, with domestic value contribution expected to increase from 
20-25% currently to around 75-80% over time, as reported by the Press Information Bureau (“PIB”), Ministry of Commerce 
and Industry 
 
• Bureau of Indian Standards (“BIS”) certification and compliance requirements : Increasingly stringent certification 
and testing requirements under the Compulsory Registration Scheme (“CRS”) are standardising product quality, safety, 
and performance across the market. Mandatory testing and prior registration enhance consumer trust a nd reduce the 
prevalence of sub -standard imports, while also creating a more level playing field that favours compliant, scaled 
manufacturers and supports adoption of high-performance, next-generation appliances 
 
• Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India initiatives: Broader policy initiatives aimed at strengthening domestic 
manufacturing and promoting localisation are supporting the development of integrated domestic ecosystems for key 
components such as motors, compressors, and electronics. These efforts are reducing  import dependence and narrowing 
the price differential between conventional and next -generation appliances, thereby improving affordability. Further,

Further, rising energy and water usage intensity of household consumption is supporting the adoption of clean technologies  
 
As appliance ownership and usage intensity rise, the lifecycle footprint of households is increasingly driven by electricity and 
water consumption sharpening the focus on resource-efficient technologies. 
 
• Rising electricity consumption and focus on energy efficiency: Residential electricity consumption reached 
approximately 334 BU in Financial Year 2022 and is projected to increase to approximately 769 BU by Financial Year 
2031P as per the Gujarat Rajya Institution for Transformation (GRIT) , highlighting the growing importance of energy 
efficiency within households. In parallel, the India Cooling Action Plan sets a target to reduce cooling energy requirements 
by 25 -40% by Financial Year 2038P, underscoring the need to reduce operating energy  consumption. This is leading  
consumers to prioritize energy -efficient appliances, with a visible shift toward higher star -rated products, particularly in 
high-usage categories such as fans and air conditioners. 
 
• Declining water availability and focus on water -efficient appliances: Declining water availability is reinforcing the 
importance of resource-efficient technologies. According to the Central Water Commission, India’s annual per capita water 
availability was approximately 1,486 cubic meters in Calendar Year 2021 and is project ed to decline to approximately 
1,367 cubic meters by Calendar Year 2031P, placing it within the water -stress threshold of below 1,700 cubic meters per 
person annually. This increases the  relevance of appliances that optimize water usage, particularly in water -intensive 
applications, driving gradual adoption of efficient, next-generation solutions 
 
Resource constraints are shifting consumer focus from upfront cost to lifecycle efficiency. Next-generation appliances are well-
positioned to benefit from this transition, as they deliver the same output with lower resource consumption.

Increasing demand across Tier 2+ cities, and performance driven differentiation are accelerating the adoption of next-generation 
consumer appliances: 
 
• Rising demand across Tier 2+ cities expanding the base of next -generation consumer appliances: Demand for next-
generation consumer appliances has historically been concentrated in Metro and Tier 1 cities. However, adoption is 
increasingly expanding across Tier 2+ cities as rising household incomes, improving residential infrastructure, and 
increasing digital access strengthen consumer purchasing power in these cities 
 
• Performance driven differentiation and upgrade -led replacement demand accelerating adoption for next -
generation consumer appliances: Consumers are increasingly prioritizing performance, functionality, convenience, and 
user experience when making purchase decisions. This shift is supported by shortening replacement cycles, particularly 
among Gen Z and young urban professionals, who are upgrading appliances more frequently (3-5 years). Next-generation 
appliances deliver measurable improvements in performance and lifecycle efficiency, strengthening their value proposition 
despite higher upfront costs and accelerating adoption. In parallel, manufacturers are investing in brand positioning and 
feature-led differentiation, supported by greater visibility into cons umer preferences through product reviews and search 
behavior. 
 
India remains underpenetrated compared to global markets across next -generation consumer appliances categories, 
indicating significant long-term headroom for growth 
 
India's consumer appliance market has evolved along a distinct path from global counterparts, with domestic incumbents 
historically prioritizing price competitiveness, distribution reach, and last -mile accessibility over technology upgrades. In 
contrast to global markets, where product roadmaps are increasingly anchored in research & development cycles, adoption of 
next-generation appliances in India has historically been moderated by longer replacement cycles and price -led purchasing 
behavior.  
 
India's operating environment adds a layer of complexity absent in most comparable markets. Indian households operate under 
distinct environmental and infrastructural conditions, including voltage fluctuations, water TDS  (“total dissolved solids ”) 
varying across the regions, and high thermal and humidity stress, which influence appliance performance and durability. A lot 
of global and incumbent players typically rely on technologies adapted from developed markets, which are often not specifically 
engineered or optimized for Indian operating conditions and consumer requirements. As domestic value addition deepens across 
critical components and sub-systems, products are being engineered to address these conditions.  
 
At the category level, adoption of next -generation technologies varies based on the degree of global integration. Categories 
with strong global prevalence, such as air conditioners, have witnessed relatively higher penetration, supported by alignment  
with global product roadmaps. In contrast, India -centric categories such as ceiling fans, MFPs, and water purifiers remain at 
earlier stages of adoption, reflecting sustained price -led competition and historically limited technology upgrades. As a result, 
while globally integrated categories are relatively mature, India -specific categories continue to represent significant headroom 
for future growth.

Within this, high -penetration categories such as fans, gas stove, and MFPs are primarily driven by upgrade -led replacement,

and intense price-led competition. 
 
Categories in the future potential zone currently have limited scope for incremental next-generation growth, where key adoption 
drivers such as intensity of consumer pain points, upgrade economics, usage intensity, and scope for visible performance 
differentiation are relatively less pronounced. As a result, adoption is more gradual today, with acceleration expected in 
subsequent waves as these drivers strengthen and upgrade triggers become more compelling.

Water purifiers represent a health-led category with low penetration but significant scope for next-generation adoption 
 
Next-generation water purifiers integrate multi -stage purification technologies spanning reverse osmosis (“RO”), ultraviolet 
(“UV”), ultrafiltration (“UF”) and mineralization with 40%+ water recovery rate when RO purification is active. It further 
enables them to differentiate through premium countertop form factors or smart monitoring capabilities such as real -time TDS 
(“Total Dissolved Solids”) tracking and filter life alerts enabling better control over maintenance. This technology -led 
architecture enabl es comprehensive contaminant removal while restoring essential minerals, delivering more consistent 
purification outcomes, improved water efficiency, and greater reliability across varying water conditions. Given water 
purification is a health-critical need, performance gaps carry greater consequence for consumers, reinforcing the prioritisation 
of purification effectiveness and driving faster upgrade cycles. This is further reinforced by increasing regulatory oversight and 
standardisation, which are improving product reliability and strengthening consumer trust in organised offerings. 
 
Next-generation water purifiers account for approximately 18% of the total market and are expected to grow at a CAGR of 29-
33% between Financial Year 2026 and Financial Year 2031P, driven by both first -time adoption and upgrade-led replacement 
with a conti nued shift toward multi -stage purification systems. Next -generation adoption is concentrated in electric purifier 
formats. Conventional next -generation electric water purifiers often apply uniform RO filtration irrespective of input water 
quality, which can result in unnecessary water wastage, removal of essential minerals, premature membrane wear and annual 
maintenance costs of ₹ 3,000–5,000 per household. Adaptive purifiers represent a niche but distinct category of water purifiers 
that continuously monitor incoming water quality and automatically select the most appropriate purification pathway. Unlike 
conventional RO systems, which route all water through  the RO membrane regardless of TDS levels, adaptive purifiers 
intelligently bypass RO when input water quality is already within acceptable limits, relying on UV and UF purification alone. 
This eliminates reject water generation, preserves essential minerals, and reduces dependency on annual maintenance contracts. 
When higher TDS levels necessitate RO pur ification, adaptive systems dynamically regulate membrane usage and recovery 
rates to maximize water utilization, minimize reject water, and extend membrane life. As a result, adaptive purifiers offer a  
more efficient, sustainable, and consumer -friendly alternative to traditional RO -based systems, particularly in regions where 
water quality varies significantly over time.

features, and reviews. While offline channels continue to account for a significant share of revenues, faster online growth 
is driving the emergence of integrated omnichannel models, where digital channels lead demand generation and conversion, 
supported by physical fulfilment and service infrastructure.

consumer discovery, comparison, and preference formation. While categories such as water purifiers continue to require

Deep-tech engineering capabilities developed in consumer appliances enable technology extensibility into proprietary 
components manufacturing for OEMs across industries 
 
Proprietary component-level technologies developed for consumer appliances form a transferable engineering foundation that 
can be deployed across adjacent industrial sectors through proprietary component manufacturing for OEMs. The strategic 
value of this participation is determined by the depth of design and IP ownership; IP -led deep-tech engineering platforms 
supplying proprietary components occupy the highest-value position in industrial supply chains, commanding entrenched OEM 
relationships, high switch ing costs, and margins driven by engineering differentiation rather than cost competition. This 
expansion diversifies revenue, reduces demand volatility through long -term OEM relationships, and creates a self-reinforcing 
capability flywheel where engineeri ng depth accumulated through proprietary component deployments feeds back into 
consumer appliance innovation. Together, consumer appliances and proprietary component manufacturing for OEMs create a 
₹ 20,202-23,031 Billion (US$ 232-265 Billion) opportunity by Financial Year 2031P. 
 
IP-led deep-tech engineering platforms create differentiated value through proprietary component supply to OEMs 
across industrial supply chains  
 
Technology extensibility enables companies to deploy core engineering -led capabilities beyond their primary consumer 
markets, with proprietary technologies developed at the component level forming a common foundation across adjacent 
applications. As these capabilities are deployed across Original Equipment Manufacturer ("OEM") supply chains, participation 
ranges from commodity component suppliers competing on cost, to contract manufacturers producing customer -specified 
designs, to IP -led proprietary deep -tech engineering platforms that own the underlying design, engineering, and intellectual 
property. The distinction in strategic value across these models is significant. Commodity suppliers compete largely on price  
with limited differentiation, while contract manufacturers execute customer designs and benefit from moderate switching costs 
driven by process familiarity. 
 
IP-led proprietary deep-tech engineering platforms own the end-to-end design, engineering, and intellectual property associated 
with critical processes,  encompassing the in -house manufacturing of engineered goods and components where product 
performance, quality, and differentiation are substantially driven by engineering design, precision manufacturing, adherence to 
specified tolerances, and compliance wi th defined qualification and testing standards. Unlike contract manufacturers that 
primarily execute to  customer specifications, these platforms proactively engineer to identify and deliver performance, 
reliability, and design improvements that the OEM may not have anticipated. This makes them strategic partners deeply 
embedded in the OEM's product development roadmap, commanding high switching costs and margins driven  by engineering 
differentiation and IP ownership. 
 
Government initiatives such as the Make in India programme and Production Linked Incentive ("PLI") schemes are supporting 
a structural shift from assembly-led manufacturing toward higher value-added components and sub-systems. As manufacturing 
ecosystems e volve beyond final -stage assembly, this is creating additional opportunities for IP -led deep -tech engineering 
platforms to participate in component design, system integration, and technology development, while strengthening domestic 
capabilities across critical engineering value chains. 
 
OEM-led demand is predominantly specification -driven, with value concentrated in high -performance components and 
integrated sub-systems. Indian OEMs increasingly rely on IP -led deep-tech engineering platforms as localized alternatives to 
imports, benefiting from faster iteration cycles and the ability to customize solutions for Indian operating conditions. Beyond 
the domestic market, these platforms are also well positioned to participate in global supply chains as OEMs pursue China+1 
diversification strategies and increasingly seek design -capable technology partners rather than purely low -cost manufacturers. 
Growing inbound engagement from domestic and global OEMs further reflects increasing recognition of India's engineering 
capabilities and serves as an early indicator of expanding demand for proprietary, technology-led solutions. 
 
These capabilities find applications across industries that are progressing along the technology evolution curve, where 
differentiation is driven by continuous performance improvements and engineering advancements.  
 
• Consumer Appliances: Large appliance categories such as washing machines, air conditioners, and refrigerators are 
increasingly adopting BLDC motors and electronically controlled systems that deliver higher energy efficiency, lower 
noise, and improved performance. As appliance architecture becomes more technology -intensive, demand for proprietary 
motors, controls, and embedded electronics is expected to increase.  
 
• Mobility & Transportation: The shift to electric vehicles is driving demand for electronically controlled thermal 
management systems, including e-compressors and cooling modules, as belt-driven mechanical systems are replaced across 
two-wheeler and four-wheeler companies. Rail transportation equipment represents an adjacent opportunity as localization 
mandates drive demand for domestically developed drive and control systems 
 
• Industrial and Energy Equipment: Solar tracking systems, industrial machinery, and energy equipment require precision 
actuator drives and control systems that deliver consistent performance under variable operating conditions. As utility -

scale installations and industrial automation expand across India, locally manufactured drive systems present a recurring 
and scalable opportunity 
 
• Aerospace, Defence, and Advanced Systems : These represent high -value, entry -barrier-driven segments where 
participation is defined by specialized engineering capabilities and the ability to meet stringent performance, reliability, 
and qualification requirements. While global players continue to do minate, domestic manufacturers are beginning to 
address capability gaps through cost-effective and locally adapted solutions

As these industries evolve, the role of engineered components becomes more critical, creating incremental opportunities to

Business model archetypes within the consumer appliance market 
 
In recent years, India’s consumer appliance market has undergone a structural shift, driven by rising household incomes, 
expanding Tier 1 and Tier 2+ cities, and increasing aspirations for home improvement and lifestyle upgrades. The emergence 
of nuclear families has further reshaped product requirements, with smaller household sizes driving demand for compact, 
efficient, and multifunctional appliances that deliver superior performance within tighter living spaces. This has further 
accelerated adoption acro ss consumer appliance categories spanning home, kitchen, air treatment, water purification, with 
purchase behaviour shifting toward higher involvement, stronger quality expectations, and more aspiration-led decision making. 
 
This transition has surfaced clear differences in how appliance brands are built and compete. The market can be mapped across 
two structural parameters: 
 
• Technology ownership: The extent to which a brand owns, outsources, or imports its core technology determines the 
sustainability of product differentiation. This ranges from brands deploying technology imported from global parents with 
limited local adaptation, to brands outsourcing core components from third-party suppliers to brands with fully proprietary 
integrated technology developed natively for Indian operating conditions  
 
• Research & development: The depth of research and development investment determines a brand's ability to continuously 
improve and compound its technology advantage. This spans brands with no independent research and development relying 
entirely on outsourced components, to brands  investing in design and product development on top of outsourced building 
blocks, to brands with sustained in -house research and development across core engineering domains including motors, 
power electronics, embedded systems, and manufacturing processes 
 
The interaction of these two parameters creates four distinct competitive models, each reflecting a different combination of 
capabilities, constraints, and growth trajectories. 
 
• Regional/Emerging Brands: Brands operating with entirely outsourced technology and no independent research and 
development investment 
 
• Traditional Incumbent Brands: Established domestic brands that source core components from proprietary component 
manufacturers but invest in design and product development on top of outsourced building blocks  
 
• Global Legacy Brands: Multinational brands that deploy technology imported from their global parent, with research and 
development limited to localisation for Indian operating conditions. While brand equity and distribution scale provide near-
term advantages, limited local engi neering depth constrains the ability to differentiate on performance or adapt rapidly to 
India-specific use cases  
 
• Deep-Tech Enabled Next-Generation Brands: Brands that own the full technology stack with sustained in -house 
research and development. This enables performance differentiation that is difficult to replicate, supports continuous 
product improvement through compounding IP, and creates a durable compe titive moat across categories 
 
Mapping these business models across technology ownership and research and development intensity highlights a largely 
unaddressed position in India's consumer appliance landscape. Consumer pain points have remained unaddressed for decades. 
Global legacy br ands possess strong research and development capabilities but primarily deploy technologies developed for 
global markets, with localization focused on adaptation rather than ground -up engineering for Indian conditions. Traditional 
incumbent and regional br ands, meanwhile, remain dependent on outsourced components and possess limited engineering 
depth. As a result, the intersection of high research and development intensity and India-first proprietary technology ownership 
remains relatively unoccupied. Deep -tech enabled next -generation brands are positioned at this intersection, with products 
engineered specifically for Indian operating conditions, usage patterns, and price -performance requirements.

Global experience shows that technology-led differentiation can transform historically commoditised appliance categories into 
premium segments through measurable improvements in performance and user experience. Brands that combine deep 
engineering ownershi p with strong product design build durable advantages, enabling continuous innovation, differentiated 
features, and sustained pricing power. 
 
This is illustrated by a global manufacturer that evolved from a single product category to a scaled, multi-category platform. A 
breakthrough in motor technology enabled differentiated products, strong consumer preference, and subsequent scale across 
both consumer and proprietary component manufacturing for OEMs. At the core is proprietary digital motor technology, with 
speeds of up to 1,25,000 RPM, enabling significant improvements in power density and miniaturisation, supported by 
approximately 6,500 engineers and integrated manufacturing. 
 
The platform was first applied to bagless vacuum cleaners, where cyclonic separation maintained consistent suction, addressing 
a key consumer pain point. Performance-led positioning enabled premium pricing, while consistent delivery built strong brand 
equity. A differentiated distribution model across 85+ markets, combining digital discovery with premium retail and demo -led 
experiences, supported conversion and repeat purchases, with consumer feedback feeding into product and engineering 
roadmaps. In parallel, entry into commercial and professional applications enabled deployment in higher -value, specification-
driven segments. This platform -led expansion across consumer and proprietary component manufacturing for OEMs drove 
sustained growth, with revenues in creasing by approximately 13x between 2006 and 2024, with above industry operating 
margins.

Threats and Challenges 
 
The Indian next generation consumer appliances market offers strong long -term growth potential, driven by rising incomes, 
increasing electrification, and growing preference for energy -efficient products. However, the sector is characterised by 
intensifying competition, supply-side dependencies, and execution complexities, which may impact the ability of technology -
led players to sustain growth, maintain differentiation, and achieve profitable scale.  
 
1. Intensifying competition and technology diffusion may reduce differentiation and pricing power:  The sector is 
witnessing heightened competition from established multinational and domestic players with strong brand equity, extensive 
distribution, and scale advantages, alongside emerging digital -first brands leveraging asset -light models, competitive 
pricing, and online channels. As adoption of energy-efficient technologies, including BLDC motors and electronic control 
systems, continues to expand, companies may need to sustain product innovation, brand positioning, and channel execution 
to maintain differentiation and command premium pricing over time. This may result in pricing pressures, higher customer 
acquisition costs, and an increasing emphasis on brand  strength, innovation, and distribution reach as key competitive 
differentiators. 
 
2. Dependence on imported electronic components exposes supply chain, cost, and currency risks:  Increasing 
electronics content has led to continued reliance on imported components such as semiconductors and controllers, exposing 
companies to global supply disruptions, geopolitical developments, and foreign exchange fluctuations. Variability in 
component availability and pricing may impact production planning and cost structures. While localisation efforts are 
progressing, limited domestic availability of high -value components may continue to pose near - to medium -term 
challenges. 
 
3. Volatility in raw material prices may impact cost structures and margins:  The industry remains sensitive to 
fluctuations in key raw materials such as steel, copper, aluminium, and plastics, driven by global commodity cycles and 
macroeconomic conditions. Changes in input costs may affect manufacturing expenses and margins, parti cularly where 
cost pass-through is constrained. Sustained volatility may require ongoing cost optimisation and sourcing efficiency . 
 
4. Execution complexities in scaling omnichannel distribution and manufacturing operations: Expansion across offline 
retail, e -commerce, and direct -to-consumer channels introduces operational complexity. Offline growth requires 
investments in distribution, inventory, and working capital, while digital channels face rising customer acquisition co sts. 
Scaling manufacturing involves challenges in capacity ramp -up, process standardisation, and maintaining product quality 
at higher volumes. Inefficiencies may impact unit economics, margins, and customer experience. 
 
5. Consumer price sensitivity and evolving demand patterns may moderate adoption of premium products:  While 
demand for energy-efficient and performance-led appliances is increasing, a significant portion of the market remains price-
sensitive, particularly in mass segments. Higher upfront costs may limit broader adoption. Evolving preferences toward 
smart and connected appliances require continuous innovation and accurate demand forecasting. Misalignment with 
consumer adoption or slower uptake in certain categories may impact growth and returns.

What we do 
 
Our business model integrates proprietary technology development, integrated manufacturing, digital -first omni -channel 
distribution, and engineering -led brand building into a replicable playbook that we apply to each product category we enter. 
Each successive category we have entered has reached meaningful commercial scale faster than the preceding one, reflecting 
increasing platform leverage, organizational learning and brand compounding.  
 
Product Development Philosophy – Solving unmet consumer pain points by leveraging our proprietary tech platform  
 
Our approach to product development is anchored in identifying product categories where we believe that consumer pain points 
are unaddressed and applying our proprietary technology platform to re-engineer these products. In each category we enter, we 
combine category selection discipline, platform leverage, consumer -first problem solving and engineering-led execution, with 
the objective of delivering step-change improvements in core performance, energy efficiency, form factor and user experience.

Fans 
 
Our fans portfolio includes ceiling fans, table fans, pedestal fans, wall fans and exhaust fans. Ceiling fans are our core pr oduct 
category within our Home Appliances segment, with a portfolio of 625 stock -keeping units (“ SKUs”) spanning price ranges 
from approximately ₹2,599 to ₹19,999. According to the Redseer Report, the fan category had remained reliant on induction 
motor technology for decades, characterized by limited or conventional aesthetics, less stable performance du ring voltage 
fluctuations, absence of connectivity and smart features, and relatively high power consumption of 50-90 watts. The ceiling fan 
category was historically dominated by induction motor technology, characterized by high power consumption, limited speed 
precision and a lack of smart features (Source: Redseer Report). We addressed this through India’s first smart and most energy-

efficient BLDC ceiling fan 8, among scaled consumer appliance companies in India (Source: Redseer Report ), delivering 
comparable airflow while consuming approximately 25 –35 watts of power (delivering 50 -60% lower power consumption), 
along with precise electronic speed control, silent operation, inverter compatibility and internet of things (“ IoT”)-enabled 
controls. We also launched India’s first BMC motor -based ceiling fan and India’s first residential BLDC ceiling fan with 
aluminum extrusion blades, India's first 5-star rated high-speed plastic BLDC pedestal fan in the 400 mm category and India’ s 
first BLDC exhaust fan across the 150mm, 200mm and 250mm categories, in each case among scaled consumer appliance 
companies in India (Source: Redseer Report).

enabled contemporary form factors including our highest -selling Renesa series and the Red Dot Design Award -winning Aris

marketplaces in India as of May 22, 2026 (Source: Redseer Report).
