Motorized food preparation 
 
Motorized food preparation (“ MFP”) appliances, including mixer grinders and cold -pressed juicers, are part of a large and 
evolving kitchen appliances category that has historically witnessed limited technology innovation, with conventional products 
often characterized by universal motors  (750-1000 watts), higher noise generation, and limited RPM settings not suited for 
Indian cooking, according to the Redseer Report. According to the Redseer Report, the diversity of Indian cuisine creates 
demand for kitchen appliances that can perform a wide variety of food preparation tasks, ranging from coarse blends and spice 
grinding to fine pastes and batter preparation. We addressed this through India’s first BLDC -powered mixer grinder, among 
scaled consumer appliance companies in India (Source: Redseer Report ), leveraging our proprietary motor and electronics 
platform to deliver intelligent coarse -mode grinding, wide RPM control, lower noise levels, compact design and smart safety 
features. We have the widest RPM operating range of 2,000 to 18,000 revolutions per minute in the mixer grinder category as 
of May 2026, offering precise control, among scaled consumer appliance companies in India (Source: Redseer Report). Our 
intelligent control systems and wide speed settings enable users to precisely control textur es from coarse blends to fine pastes, 
while delivering grinding performance comparable to conventional higher -wattage mixer grinders. We also introduced, in 
March 2024, India’s first BLDC-powered mixer grinder with a non-geared chopper attachment, India’s first mixer grinder with 
auto detection for chopper and non -chopper attachments and In dia’s first mixer grinder with an advanced safety system 
comprising overload protection, interface error detection, anti -gravity lid locks and no self -start functionality upon restoration 
of power after an outage, in each case among scaled consumer appliance companies in India (Source: Redseer Report). 
 
 
Source: Redseer Report

historically been associated with several consumer pain points, including the application of uniform RO filtration irrespecti ve 
of input water quality, resulting in the inappropriate use of RO purification in certain water conditions, high water wastage and 
removal of essential minerals, high AMC costs and lock ins, and limited transparency around filter replacement requirements

Kitchen Appliances

relating to grinding consistency, safety and versatility. These products use electronically controlled motors with a wide 
speed range and include a proprietary low-speed “Coarse Mode” to support both fine grinding and coarse textures typically

functionality to reduce clogging, a 121 mm hopper, simplified assembly and cleaning, hopper -lock detection, auto -lid 
detection, no-auto-restart after power interruptions and LED status indicators. Our products support extraction across fruit 
juices, vegetable juices and nut milks.

associated with traditional water purifiers, which according to the Redseer Report, include filter replacement transparency,

adaptive RO water purifier that analyzes source water TDS and engages RO filtration based on input water quality, upon 
TDS exceeding specified thresholds. Our products enable users to monitor filter health status and replacement requirements

Manufacturing operations at our Chakan Facility comprise mechanical, electrical and sub -assembly processes.

Supply Chain and Logistics Network 
 
Our supply chain and logistics network supports raw material procurement, manufacturing, warehousing, order fulfillment, 
distribution and after -sales service flows for our consumer appliances business. The network comprises our manufacturing 
facilities in Pune, Maharashtra, a mother warehouse in Pune, Maharashtra, seven regional warehouses across India, 
transportation arrangements across primary, secondary and last -mile legs, and channel -specific fulfillment arrangements for

254 
offline, online, quick-commerce and direct-to-consumer sales. These operations are supported by enterprise resource planning, 
warehouse management, transportation management, demand forecasting and order management systems.  
 
Raw Materials 
 
Our manufacturing operations require raw materials, components and sub -assemblies across electrical, electronic, mechanical, 
plastic and magnetic categories. These include, among others, copper, steel, aluminum, plastic resins and molded plastic 
components, magnets, printed circuit boards, semiconductors, integrated circuits, other electronic components, motor 
components, controllers, wires and harnesses and packaging materials. The specific input mix varies by product category, as 
set out below.  
 
• Fans require inputs such as motors, PCBs, magnets, metal and plastic components, blades and related hardware.  
• Mixer grinders and juicers require motors, electronic components, jars, blades, plastic and metal enclosures and safety -
related components.  
• Water purifiers require filtration materials, pumps, tanks, electronic control systems and other water circuit components.  
• Our proprietary components manufactured for enterprise customers require inputs such as electronic components, copper, 
stators, rotors, magnets, molding compounds, PCB substrates and related assemblies.  
 
We procure raw materials and components from domestic and overseas suppliers, based on factors such as product 
specifications, availability, pricing, quality, delivery timelines and continuity of supply. Certain inputs, including electr onic 
components, sem iconductors, magnets and specialized filtration components, may be sourced through globally integrated 
supply chains, either directly or through domestic suppliers.  
 
Our purchases are generally undertaken on a purchase order basis, with commercial terms agreed for each purchase or series of 
purchases, including specifications, price, quantity, delivery timelines, payment terms and quality requirements. In certain cases, 
we may enter into supply or pricing arrangements to secure availability or pricing for periods up to one year.  
 
Our procurement and sourcing decisions are influenced by product development requirements, production plans, demand 
forecasts, input price trends, supplier capacity, lead times, exchange rate movements and availability of technically qualifi ed 
alternatives. For certain inputs, we also work with suppliers during product development to identify materials, grades, finishes 
and processes that meet the design, performance and cost requirements of our products.  
 
We have also undertaken selected backward integration initiatives in relation to manufacturing processes, including in -house 
paint shop operations and injection molding for select plastic components used across product categories. These initiatives 
reduce dependence on external suppliers for certain processed components and provide greater control over selected 
manufacturing inputs. However, we continue to rely on third-party suppliers for a significant portion of raw materials, bought-
out components and sub-assemblies used in our products. 
 
Power, fuel and water requirements 
 
Our manufacturing facilities require power, fuel and water for manufacturing operations, utility systems, testing processes, 
facility maintenance and employee welfare requirements. Power is used for assembly lines, EMS operations, motor assembly, 
injection molding, painting, testing equipment, compressed air systems, lighting, HVAC and other facility utilities. Fuel 
requirements primarily relate to paintshop and molding operations, including facility utilities. Water is used for domestic 
consumption, facility maintenance and selected manufacturing and utility processes, including paintshop and molding related 
operations, where applicable.

holding and replenishment location. Our warehousing network follows a hub -and-spoke model comprising one mother

and Chennai, as of March 31, 2026. Our mother warehouse has a storage capacity of 600,000 units, while the seven regional

Technology 
 
Our technology platform comprises motors, power electronics, control systems, embedded software, connectivity and industrial 
design. We use this platform across our Consumer Appliances Business and Proprietary Components segments, with 
adaptations based on  product-specific requirements, including power rating, torque profile, speed range, duty cycle, thermal 
conditions, form factor, user interface, connectivity and applicable regulatory standards. This platform is used in products such 
as fans, mixer grinde rs, water purifiers, smart locks and cold -pressed juicers, and in components such as motors, controllers 
and electronic assemblies supplied to enterprise customers. 
 
Motor platform 
 
Our motor platform is built around electrically commutated motor and BLDC motor technology, with motor designs configured 
for different voltage, power, torque, speed and thermal requirements. The platform includes low-voltage and high-voltage motor 
designs, with applications across consumer appliances and enterprise components. Our motor and motor -driver capabilities 
cover voltage configurations ranging from 12V to 24V at the low -voltage end and 200V to 450V at the high -voltage end, and 
power ratings ranging from 6W to 1,000W. These capabilities allow us to select motor architecture and motor -driver topology 
based on the application, such as ceiling fans, exhaust fans, mixer grinders and enterprise components.  
 
Our motor development has evolved across successive generations of BLDC fan motors, with improvements in 
manufacturability, electronics hardware protections, motor control algorithms, reduction in motor diameter, reduction in stee l 
use, introduction of plastic-grade bottom diffuser, smart IoT integration, use of NdFeB magnets, integration of electronics inside 
the motor casing, BMC ceiling fan motor architecture, and reduction in motor diameter and volume in later generations.  
  
Power electronics 
 
Our power electronics capabilities are designed to support product efficiency, durability and adaptability across operating 
conditions such as high temperatures, humidity, voltage fluctuations and lightning surges. Our hardware architecture has 
evolved from supporting input voltage of up to 285 Vac in Generation 1 products to up to 440 Vac in subsequent generations, 
together with improvements in surge protection capabilities from 2 kV to up to 10 kV in select configurations.  
 
Our systems are designed for sustained operation under elevated temperatures, supported by component -level stress analysis, 
in-house reliability testing and power -efficient hardware architectures. We have improved electronics efficiency through 
component selection, circuit design and system -level architecture, while standardizing hardware designs across a majority of 
our product portfolio to improve reusability, simplify manufacturing and servicing, and support product development timelines. 
 
Control systems and firmware 
 
Our control systems and in -house firmware capabilities support speed control, product performance and reliability across 
varying usage conditions, and enable integration with our hardware and software components. These capabilities allow us to 
design and deploy motor-driver topologies and architectures across low-voltage and high-voltage motor designs, power ratings 
ranging from 6W to 1,000W, discrete and integrated controller solutions, sensor and sensor -less drivers, and sine, trapezoidal 
and field-oriented control topologies. 
Our design framework allows us to tailor motor and driver topology selection to specific product requirements, including for 
ceiling fans, exhaust fans and mixer grinders. Our in-house firmware architecture also supports migration across semiconductor 
platforms, which may help reduce dependency on specific components and address supply constraints. Production traceability 
between PCBAs and finished products further supports quality monitoring and product reliability across categories.  
  
Software and connectivity 
 
Our software and connectivity capabilities comprise embedded firmware, connected -product features and IoT and cloud 
infrastructure supporting select products across our portfolio. These capabilities support product functions such as remote 
control, third-party smart assistant integration, device diagnostics, usage-related features and over-the-air updates. 
 
We have developed significant elements of our smart product ecosystem in-house, including Wi-Fi controller firmware, server 
connectivity, cloud data management, user interfaces and background services. This enables us to provide connected -product 
functionality on select models and to deploy software updates and feature enhancements after product sale. As of March 31, 
2026, we had over 500,000 connected devices on our cloud platform.  
 
Our connected -product platform also provides product and usage data that may be used, subject to applicable law and our 
internal policies, to analyze user activity, identify service issues and support product development and customer support.

257 
Industrial design 
 
Industrial design forms part of our technology platform and is used in the development of product form, color, material, finish, 
tactile elements, control interfaces and display logic. Our design approach is intended to align product engineering with 
manufacturable form factors and user interfaces across product categories. We also have an in-house design studio and a design 
process covering concept development, prototyping, design validation and design -for-manufacture handoff.  
 
Our design process is supported by prototyping and simulation capabilities. Our proto -shop includes 24 3D printers capable of 
printing various materials and finishes, and light simulation software is used to evaluate interface and lighting design conc epts 
before investment in molds and parts. These tools support product design iteration and validation of shape, color, material, 
finish and user-interface features. 
 
Modular product architecture 
 
Our product portfolio is developed on a modular architecture comprising five core building blocks: motor platform, power 
electronics, control system and firmware, software and connectivity, and industrial design. Each module is developed, validated 
and mai ntained so that it can be configured, recombined or adapted across product categories, subject to product -specific 
engineering and regulatory requirements. This enables common technology elements to be reused across products while 
allowing category-specific development for mechanical design, thermal management, safety, water circuit design, user interface 
and other product-level requirements.  
 
For mixer grinders, we utilized motor platform and power electronics learnings from our ceiling fans, including motor control  
strategies, drive circuit topologies and protection logic, and adapted them for high -torque and intermittent-load requirements. 
For water purifiers, design language, interface elements, IoT connectivity and over -the-air update capability draw on the same 
cloud and firmware infrastructure used across other connected products, while category -specific engineering is focused on 
water circuit design, purification stack integration and regulatory compliance.  
 
Integration with manufacturing 
 
Our technology platform is integrated with our manufacturing processes through in -house and facility-level capabilities across 
process engineering, motor assembly, PCB assembly, injection molding, painting, assembly operations, testing and traceability. 
Our manufacturing facilities use SAP ERP, manufacturing execution systems and related tools to connect raw material 
management, inventories, finance, assembly lines, warehousing and quality functions. These systems support production data 
capture, traceability and monitoring across manufacturing processes.  
 
Our manufacturing and technology teams use production-line data, testing data and service feedback to support design iteration, 
component selection and process improvements. This integration is relevant to both consumer appliances and proprietary 
components, where product performance depends on alignment between product design, electronics architecture, motor design, 
firmware, assembly processes and testing parameters.

Our research and development function supports product development, technology development, platform extension, testing, 
validation and design-for-manufacture across our Consumer Appliances Business and Proprietary Components segments. Our 
R&D activities are focused on motors, power electronics, control systems, embedded software, connectivity, industrial design, 
mechanical engineering, product reliability, materials, simulation and testing. We use our R&D capabilities to develop new

user interfaces, lighting effects, packaging and related design elements. These tools support coordination between industrial  
design, mechanical e ngineering, electronics, firmware and manufacturing teams from concept stage through engineering

and vibration testing, automated testing stations, barcode or QR-code based traceability, vision-based inspection systems, ERP-
enabled quality modules and statistical process control tools to monitor selected production and quality parameters. Our quality 
infrastructure includes equipment such as 3D scanning systems, coordinate measuring machines, vision -based inspection 
systems and reliability testing equipment.

Customer Support and Resolution Mechanism 
 
We provide customer support for installation, warranty-related service, repairs, product queries and after-sales services through 
our customer support channels and service network. Customers may register service requests through IVR, online chatbots, our 
website, e-mail or our consumer grievance contact number, contact our customer support team at 84484 49442 or write to us at 
support@atomberg.com. Service requests are tracked through our internal systems and routed to our customer experience team,

completion. Area Service Partners maintain defined quantities of fast-moving spare parts to support same-visit closure of service 
complaints. Where a required spare part is unavailable at the Area Service Partner level, the part is sourced from the mapped 
regional warehouse or, where necessary, from the mother warehouse. For connected products, app -based diagnostics, device-
level data  and over -the-air update capability may also be used to identify issues and support resolution. We use customer 
complaints, service requests, warranty claims and field feedback to identify recurring issues and support product, process an d 
quality improvements.

Laws in relation to our business 
 
The Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 (the “BIS Act”) and Bureau of Indian Standards Rules, 201  (the “BIS Rules”) 
 
The BIS Act and the BIS Rules provide for the establishment of standards for goods, articles, processes, systems and services , 
indicative of the quality and specification (“Indian Standard ”) and for the grant of licences to use the Bureau of Indian 
Standards Certification Mark (the “ Standard Mark ”) by the Bureau of Indian Standards (the “ BIS”). A licence from the 
Director General of BIS is required to be obtained by the applicable entities before manufacturing, selling, storing for sale, 
distributing or importing any goods notified under the BIS Act for mandatory BIS certification. BIS is empowered to inspect  
premises, draw and test samples, and seize goods and articles to enf orce the provisions of the BIS Act . Certification officers 
appointed by the BIS are empowered to require any person engaged in the manufacture, storage, sale or distribution of goods 
covered by the BIS Act to furnish information and samples in relation to such goods, to inspect any books or documents, to 
search any premises and to se ize goods in the event of contravention of the BIS Act or any quality control order notified 
thereunder. Any use of the Standard Mark on goods not conforming to the relevant Ind ian Standard, or any misuse of the 
Standard Mark without a valid BIS licence, attracts penalties under the BIS Act.  
 
The Legal Metrology Act, 200  (the “Legal Metrology Act”) and the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 
(the “Packaged Commodities Rules”) 
 
The Legal Metrology Act establishes and enforces standards of weights and measures and regulates trade and commerce in 
goods sold or distributed by weight, measure or number. The Legal Metrology Act and rules framed thereunder regulate, inter 
alia, the labelling and packaging of commodities, notification of government -approved test centres for verification of weights 
and measures used and lists penalties for offences and compounding of offences under it. All weights and measures used in our 
Company's manufacturing and sales operations are required to be verified, stamped and sealed by the prescribed authority. Any 
non-compliance or violation under the Legal Metrology Act may result in, inter alia, a monetary penalty on the manufacturer 
or seizure of goods or imprisonment in certain cases. The Legal Metrology Act is administered and enforced by the Controller 
of Legal Metrology at the national level and by state -level Directorates of Legal Metrology; their o fficers are empowered to 
inspect, seize and test weights, measures and pre-packaged commodities. 
 
The Packaged Commodities Rules , framed under the Legal Metrology Act , prescribe mandatory declarations on the package 
of every pre-packaged commodity, including the name and address of the manufacturer or packer, the net quantity, the month 
and year of manufacture, the maximum retail price and consumer care details. The Pac kaged Commodities Rules also require 
manufacturers and packers to obtain registration with the applicable authority within ninety days of commencing  pre-packing 
or import of commodities for sale. It further requires that all mandatory declarations be displayed at the point of sale on the 
product listing pages of e-commerce platforms through which pre-packaged commodities are offered for sale, including through 
any online marketplace or direct-to-consumer digital channels.  
 
The Consumer Protection Act, 201  (the “Consumer Protection Act”) and the Consumer Protection (E -Commerce) Rules, 
2020 (the “E-Commerce Rules”)  
 
The Consumer Protection Act provides for the protection of consumer interests against deficiencies in goods and services, 
unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements, and establishes consumer disputes redressal commissions at the  
district, state and national levels for the redressal of consumer grievances. The Central Consumer Protection Authority (the 
“CCPA”), constituted under section 10 of the Consumer Protection Act, is empowered to investigate violations, recall unsafe 
goods or order the withdrawal of unsafe services, and impose penalties for false or misleading advertisements.  
 
The Consumer Protection Act imposes product liability on manufacturers, product sellers and product service providers in 
respect of any harm caused to a consumer by a defective product or deficiency in services. A product manufacturer is liable

266 
where the product contains a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from manufacturing specifications or express 
warranty, does not contain adequate instructions for correct use so as to prevent harm, or does not conform to the express 
warranty made by the manufacturer. Manufacturers and advertisers are required to ensure that any claims relating to a product’s 
characteristics are accurate, capable of substantiation, and are not false or misleading within the meaning of the Consumer 
Protection Act and relevant guidelines issued by the Central Consumer Protection Authority.  
 
The E-Commerce Rules, issued under the Consumer Protection Act, apply to goods and services bought or sold over digital or 
electronic networks and specify the duties of sellers and the duties and liabilities of e -commerce entities. To the extent that the 
products are sold through direct-to-consumer digital platform s and through third -party e-commerce marketplaces, the sellers 
are required to comply with the applicable obligations prescribed for sellers and e -commerce entities under the E -Commerce 
Rules, inc luding disclosure, grievance redressal, and return policy obligations. The E -Commerce Rules impose distinct 
obligations on sellers and on e -commerce entities, including requirements relating to disclosure of seller details, appointment 
of a grievance officer and prohibition of unfair trade practices. 
 
The Sale of Goods Act, 1 30 (the “Sale of Goods Act”) 
 
The Sale of Goods Act  governs contracts for the sale of goods in India, including the conditions and warranties applicable to 
the sale of goods, the transfer of property and title between buyer and seller, rights and duties arising on delivery, and remedies 
available to buyers and sellers in the event of breach. The contracts for sale of goods are subject to the general principles of the 
law relating to contracts i.e., the Indian Contract Act, 1872. A contract for sale of goods has, however, certain peculiar features 
such as, transfer of ownership of the goods, delivery of goods, rights and duties of the buyer and seller, remedies for breac h of 
contract, conditions and warranties implied under a contract for sale of goods, etc. which are the subject matter of the provision 
of the Sale of Goods Act. 
 
The Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1 51 (the “IDR Act”) 
 
The IDR Act provides for the development and regulation of certain specified industries and empowers the Central Government 
to regulate those industries through a system of licensing and registration. An industrial undertaking that is exempt from 
licensing under the IDR Act is required to file an Industrial Entrepreneurs' Memorandum (“ IEM”) with the Secretariat for 
Industrial Assistance, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (“ DPIIT”), Ministry of Commerce and 
Industry, and, upon acknowledgement of such filing, no further approval under the IDR Act is required in respect of the activities 
covered by the IEM subject to applicable conditions and exemptions. 
 
The Electricity Act, 2003 (the “Electricity Act”) and the Central Electricity Authority (Measures relating to Safety and 
Electric Supply) Regulations, 2023 (the “CEA Regulations”) 
 
The Electricity Act govern s the generation, transmission, distribution, trading and use of electricity, providing for, inter alia, 
the development of the electricity industry and power system, promotion of competition, consumer protection, rationalisation 
of tariffs, transparent subsidy policies, promotion of efficient and environmentally friendly policies, and the constitution of the 
Central Electricity Authority ( “CEA”), regulatory commissions and an appellate tribunal . The CEA’s functions include, inter 
alia, (a) specifying technical standards for construction of electrical plants, electric lines and grid connectivity; (b) spe cifying 
grid standards for operation and maintenance of transmission lines; and (c) advising the Government and appropriate 
commissions on all technical matters relating to the generation, transmission and distribution of electricity; the Electricity Act 
also provides for a Central Electricity Regulatory Commission ( “CERC”) and a State Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(“SERC”) for each state. CERC is responsible for (a) regulating inter-state transmission of electricity; (b) determining tariff for 
inter-state transmission of electricity; (c) issuing licences to function as a transmission licensee; and (d) specifying and enforcing 
standards with respect to the quality, continuity and reliability of service by a licensee, with SERCs performing similar functions 
at the state level and also being required to promote co -generation and generation of electricity from renewable sources, 
including by specifying a renewable purchase percentage for distribution licensees in their respective areas .  
 
The CEA Regulations apply to electrical installations (including electrical plant and electric lines) and persons engaged in 
generation, transmission, distribution, trading, supply or use of electricity . The CEA Regulations set out general safety 
requirements requiring all electric supply lines and apparatus to be appropriately rated, of sufficient mechanical strength, and 
constructed, installed, protected, worked and maintained so as to ensure the safety o f human beings, animals and property.

The EP Act provides for the protection and improvement of the environment and empowers the Central Government to take all

contravention, and in the event of contravention continuing beyond a period of one year, with imprisonment for a term which 
may extend to seven years. 
 
The EP Rules prescribe the standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from industries, operations or 
processes and impose prohibitions and restrictions on the location of industries and on the handling of hazardous substances in

of legislation enacted to take appropriate steps for the preservation of the earth’s natural resources, which, among other th ings, 
includes the preservation of air quality and control of air pollution. The Air Act requires any individual, industry, or institution 
responsible for emitting smoke or gases by way of fuel use or chemical reactions to apply in the prescribed form and obtain

The Trade Marks Act, 1    (the “Trade Marks Act”) and the Trade Marks Rules, 2017 (the “Trade Marks Rules”)  
 
The Trade Marks Act provides for the registration and protection of trademarks in India and prescribes civil and criminal

The Patents Act provides for the grant, registration and enforcement of patents in India and empowers the Controller General

Competition law 
 
The Competition Act, 2002 (the “Competition Act”) as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 (the 
“Amendment Act”) 
 
The Competition Act prohibits anti -competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position and combinations that cause or are 
likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India. Anti -competitive agreements include horizontal 
agreements be tween competitors relating to price -fixing, bid -rigging, market allocation and output restriction, which are 
presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition. The Competition Commission of India (“CCI”) is the statutory 
authority responsible for the enforcement of the Competition Act and is empowered to investigate violations, impose penalties 
and direct divestiture or other structural remedies. 
 
The Amendment Act introduced a deal -value threshold for combination notifications, applicable where the value of the 
transaction exceeds ₹20,000.00 million and the enterprise being acquired, taken over, merged, or amalgamated has substantial 
business operations in India. The Amendment Act reduced the outer merger review timeline from 210 days to 150 days, which 
revised timeline was brought into force with effect from September 10, 2024. Additionally, the Amendment Act empowers the 
CCI to appoint a Director General, with the prior approval of the Central Government, for the purposes of conducting 
investigations into alleged contraventions of the Competition Act. Our Company is required to ensure that its pricing, 
distribution and commercial arrangements comply with the Competition Act and to file the requisite notifications with the CCI 
in connection with any qualifying combinations involving our Company. 
 
The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 also expanded the definition of “ cartel” to include hub -and-spoke arrangements, 
where a trade association, intermediary, or consultant facilitates coordination among competitors, even where such person is 
not itself a competitor. Under the amended definition of cartel, a person who is not engag ed in identical or similar trade of 
goods or services may nonetheless be held liable if it participates or intends to participate in the furtherance of an anti -
competitive agreeme nt between competitors. In addition, the prohibition on anti -competitive vertical agreements has been 
broadened by replacing the concept of “exclusive supply agreement” with “exclusive dealing agreement”, which now captures 
both the supply side and the acquisition side of such arrangements. Distribution agreements, dealer agreements, and channel 
partner arrangements entered into by our Company for the sale of its products through offline and online channels, as well as 
supply agreements entered into by our Company, are required to be reviewed for compliance with these provisions. 
 
Technology, data and cybersecurity related laws 
 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 (the “IT Act”) and the Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices and 
Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011 (“IT Security Rules”)  
 
The IT Act aims to provide legal recognition to transactions carried out by various means of electronic data interchange and 
other means of electronic communication and facilitate electronic filing of documents. The IT Act creates a constructive 
mechanism for the authentication of electronic documentation through digital signatures. The IT Act makes electronic 
commerce seamless by recognizing contracts concluded through electronic means, protects intermediaries in respect of third -
party information liability. The IT Security Rules enlist directions for the disclosure, collection, storage and transfer of sensitive 
personal data by a body corporate or any person acting on behalf of a body corporate. The IT Security Rules require every such 
body corporate or person, who on behalf of the body corporate receives, stores or handles information to provide a privacy 
policy for handling and dealing with personal information, including sensitive personal data publishing such policy on its 
website. The IT Security Rules further require that all such personal data be used solely for the purposes for w hich it was 
collected, and any third -party disclosure of such data is made with the prior consent of the information provider, unless 
contractually agreed upon between them or where such disclosure is mandated by law.  
 
The Information Technology (Intermediaries Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Intermediaries 
Rules”) 
 
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has also notified the IT Intermediaries Rules under the IT Act, in 
supersession of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2011, requiring intermediaries receiving, storing, 
transmitting, or providing any service with respect to electro nic messages to not knowingly host, publish, transmit, select or 
modify any information prohibited under the IT Intermediaries Rules, to disable hosting, publishing, transmission, selection or 
modification of such information once they become aware of it, as well as specifying the due diligence to be observed by 
intermediaries. The IT Intermediaries Rules also make it mandatory for an intermediary to publish its privacy policy, rules, and

and platforms was announced under the IT Act and the IT Intermediaries Rules instructing intermediaries and platforms to

AI, software, or algorithms to users in India only after accurately labelling the generated output. Additionally, they must l abel 
all artificially generated media and text with unique identifiers or metadata to facilitate easy identification. 
 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (“DPDP Act”)  
 
The DPDP Act received the assent of the President of India on August 11, 2023. It seeks to provide for the processing of digital 
personal data in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need to process such 
personal data for lawful and other incidental purposes. It defines personal data to mean any data about an individual who is 
identifiable by or in relation to such data (“ Personal Data”). It further defines a data fiduciary to mean any person who alon e 
or in conjunction with other persons determines the purpose and means of processing of personal data (“Data Fiduciary”), and 
a data principal to mean an individual to whom the Personal Data relates (“Data Principal”). 
 
The DPDP Act applies to the processing of digital Personal Data within India where the Personal Data is collected in digital 
form or where it is collected in a non-digital form and is subsequently digitised. It also applies to processing of digital Personal 
Data outside of India, if such processing is in connection with any activity related to offering of goods or services to Data  
Principals within India. The DPDP Act does not apply to Personal Data processed by an individual for any personal or domestic 
purpose, and Personal Data that is made publicly available by the Data Principal to whom such personal data relates or any 
other person who is under an obligation under any law for the time being in force in India to make such Personal Data publicly 
available. As per the DPDP Act, a person may process the Personal Data of a Data Principal for a lawful purpose, for which the 
Data Principal has given their consent or for certain legitimate uses. It also provides for the establishment of a Data Protection 
Board of India for taking remedial actions and imposing penalties for breach of the provisions of the DPDP Act. It imposes 
restrictions and obligations on Data Fiduciaries in relation to dealing with personal data and levies penalties for breach of  
obligations prescribed under the DPDP Act.  
 
The Central Government is considering enacting legislation for non -personal data (“NPD”). In September 2019, the Ministry 
of Electronics and Information Technology established the NPD Committee to propose regulations for NPD. The committee 
has released two reports suggesting frameworks for NPD governance, access, sharing, and a registration  regime for data 
businesses. In May 2022, a draft National Data Governance Framework was issued, aiming to mobilize non -personal data for 
public and private use, proposing a non-personal data-based India datasets program and outlining rules for secure access by the 
research and innovation ecosystem. 
 
The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 
 
The Indian Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 
(“DPDP Rules”) on November 14, 2025. The DPDP Rules aim to operationalise the DPDP Act and regulate the processing of 
personal data in India, ensuring individuals ’ privacy rights are protected. The DPDP Rules are applicable for a limited set of 
governance and institutional provisions being effective immediately, consent management related stipulations come into effect 
after 12 months a nd the substantive obligations will take effect after 18 months. The DPDP Rules introduce, among others, 
clear privacy notices, prescriptive security safeguards, breach -reporting timelines, data -retention limits and provisions for 
protection for children and vulnerable persons.

Main objects of our Company  
 
The main objects contained in our Memorandum of Association are as follows: 
 
“1. To manufacture, produce, prepare, assemble, heat, grade, mould, cast, buy, sell, resale, import, export, store, forward, 
distribute, dispose of, develop, handle, market, supply or otherwise to deal in all types of mechanical, electronic, electrical 
or technological appliances, goods, merchandise, articles, machinery, equipment, devices capable of being run on BLDC 
motor or otherwise such as ceiling fans, rotators, transformers, air conditioners, air treatment or circulation related 
products, consumer electr onics and allied products which may include integration of such products over a physical or 
technology platform and to carry on in India or elsewhere, the business of manufacturers, producers, processors, 
exporters, buyers, sellers, traders, distributors, fabricators, assemblers, fitters, installers, repairers, agents and dealers 
in electrical, electronics and mechanical engineering items including fans, motors, pumps, generator sets, and all types 
of electrical, mechanical, chemical, electro -mechanical & e lectronic items, and spare parts, accessories used for 
industrial, domestic and agricultural purposes and activities connected therewith or ancillary thereof . 
 
2.  To carry on the business of manufacturing assembling, altering, exchanging, buying, selling, importing, exporting and 
otherwise dealing in consumer durables, kitchen appliances and home appliances including but not limited to gas stove, 
mixer-grinder, juicers, blenders, microwave, dishwashers, water purifiers, sandwich makers, atta makers, electric kettles, 
air fryers, induction, OTG’s, vacuum cleaner, air purifiers, all types of irons, steamers, toasters, pressure cooker, rice 
cooker, air conditioners,  coolers, refrigerator, water heaters, TV and other related appliances, apparatus, instruments, 
equipment’s and devices for amusement and entertainment, electronic goods required in any trade, industry and all kinds 
of electronic accessories, appliances, i mplements, components, instruments, equipment’s stores and spares, spare parts, 
devices, contrivances, apparatus and supplies related to or connected with the aforesaid, and all such electronic goods 
adapted, invented and discovered in future.”       
 
The main objects as contained in our Memorandum of Association enable our Company to carry on the business presently being 
carried on and proposed to be carried on by our Company.

DIVIDEND POLICY 
The dividend distribution policy of our Company was approved and adopted by our Board on July 22, 2026 (the “Dividend 
Distribution Policy”). The declaration and payment of dividends on our Equity Shares, if any, will be recommended by our 
Board and approved by our Shareholders, at their discretion, subject to the provisions of the Articles of Association and the  
Companies Act, including the rules made thereunder and other relevant laws, rules and regulations, each as amended. Further, 
the Board shall also have the absolute power to declare interim dividend in compliance with the Companies Act.  
 
Any future determination as to quantum of dividend, if any, will be at the discretion of the Board and will depend on a number 
of internal and external factors. Some of the financial/internal factors on the basis of which our Company may declare dividend 
shall, inter alia, include profits earned and available for distribution, accumulated reserves including retained earnings, earnings 
outlook for next three to five years, liquidity position including our present and expected obligations, expected future capital 
expenditure requirements including organic/inorganic  growth opportunities, organic growth plans and expansion, long -term 
investments proposed, including capital restructuring and debt reduction, cost of raising funds from alternate sources , 
crystallisation of contingent liabilities, profit earned for the year, past dividend trends of the Company and the industry, financial 
commitments of the Company with respect to the outstanding borrowings and interest thereon, current and projected cash 
balances and cash flows of the Company, other corporate action options available to the Company (including bonus issue, buy-
back of shares, etc.) and any other relevant factors and material events. The external factors on the basis of which our Company 
may declare the dividend include but are not limited to significant changes in the macroeconomic environment, the introduction 
of new regulatory requirements or material changes in the existing taxation or regulatory regime, technological changes 
necessitating new investment, the state of the economy and capital markets requiring our Company to maintain liquidity, the 
rate of inflation, applicable taxes, including dividend distribution tax, and any other relevant factors and material events,  
including statutory and contractual restrictions, as may be deemed fit by the Board.   
 
Our Company has not declared any dividends on the Equity Shares or Preferences Shares of our Company during the Financial 
Years ended March 31, 2024, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026, and from April 1, 2026 up to the date of this Draft Red 
Herring Prospectus. 
 
There is no guarantee that any dividends will be declared or paid in the future. Our Company may retain all future earnings, if 
any, for use in the operations and expansion of our business. For further details, see “Risk Factors — We cannot assure payment

The Group segregates assets and liabilities into current and non-current categories for presentation in the balance sheet after considering its normal operating cycle and
other criteria set out in Ind AS 1, “Presentation of Financial Statements”. For this purpose, current assets and liabilities include the current portion of non-current assets
and liabilities respectively.
As per Ind AS 1, para 66, the Group shall classify an asset as current when: 
(a) it expects to realise the asset, or intends to sell or consume it, in its normal operating cycle; 
(b) it holds the asset primarily for the purpose of trading; 
(c) it expects to realise the asset within twelve months after the reporting period; or 
(d) the asset is cash or a cash equivalent unless the asset is restricted from being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at least twelve months after the reporting
period. 
All other assets are classified as non-current
Intra-group balances and transactions, and any unrealised income and expenses arising from intragroup transactions, are eliminated.
As per Ind AS 1, para 69, the Group shall classify a liability as current when: 
(a) it expects to settle the liability in its normal operating cycle; 
(b) it holds the liability primarily for the purpose of trading; 
(c) the liability is due to be settled within twelve months after the reporting period; or
(d) it does not have the right at the end of the reporting period to defer settlement of the liability for at least twelve months after the reporting period.
The terms of the liability that could, at the option of the counterparty, result in its settlement by the issue of equity instruments do not affect its classification.
Based on the nature of products / activities of the group and the normal time between acquisition of assets and their realisation in cash or cash equivalents, the group
has determined its operating cycle as a period not exceeding twelve months for the purpose of classification of its assets and liabilities as current and non-current.
The Group measures financial instruments at fair value at each balance sheet date.
Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement
date. The fair value measurement is based on the presumption that the transaction to sell the asset or transfer the liability takes place either:
►	In the principal market for the asset or liability, or
►	In the absence of a principal market, in the most advantageous market for the asset or liability
The principal or the most advantageous market must be accessible by the Group.
The fair value of an asset or a liability is measured using the assumptions that market participants would use when pricing the asset or liability, assuming that market
participants act in their economic best interest.
A fair value measurement of a non-financial asset takes into account a market participant’s ability to generate economic benefits by using the asset in its highest and best
use or by selling it to another market participant that would use the asset in its highest and best use.
The Group uses valuation techniques that are appropriate in the circumstances and for which sufficient data are available to measure fair value, maximising the use of
relevant observable inputs and minimising the use of unobservable inputs.
The Group classifies all other liabilities as non-current.

Impairment exists when the carrying value of an asset or cash generating unit exceeds its recoverable amount, which is the higher of its fair value less costs of disposal
and its value in use. The fair value less costs of disposal calculation is based on available data from binding sales transactions, conducted at arm’s length, for similar
assets or observable market prices less incremental costs for disposing of the asset. The value in use calculation is based on a DCF model. The cash flows are derived
from the budget for the next five years. The recoverable amount is sensitive to the discount rate used for the DCF model as well as the expected future cash-inflows and
the growth rate used for extrapolation purposes. These estimates are most relevant to goodwill and other intangibles with indefinite useful lives recognised by the
Group.
Intangible assets
Intangible assets acquired separately are measured on initial recognition at cost. Following initial recognition, intangible assets are carried at cost less accumulated
amortisation. An intangible asset is recognized, where it is probable that the future economic benefits attributable to the asset will flow to the enterprise and where its
cost can be reliably measured. The group capitalises software costs where it is reasonably estimated that the software has an enduring useful life. 
Intangible assets with finite lives are amortised on a straight line basis over the useful economic life and assessed for impairment whenever there is an indication that
the intangible asset may be impaired. The amortisation period and the amortisation method for an intangible asset with a finite useful life are reviewed at least at the
end of each reporting period. Changes in the expected useful life or the expected pattern of consumption of future economic benefits embodied in the asset are
considered to modify the amortisation period or method, as appropriate, and are treated as changes in accounting estimates. The amortisation expense on intangible
assets with finite lives is recognised in the statement of profit and loss unless such expenditure forms part of carrying value of another asset.
Estimated useful life of software is 3 years and it is amortized basis straight line  method.
An intangible asset is derecognised upon disposal (i.e., at the date the recipient obtains control) or when no future economic benefits are expected from its use or
disposal. Gains or losses arising from the de-recognition of an intangible asset are measured as the difference between the net disposal proceeds and the carrying
amount of the asset and are recognised in the statement of profit and loss when the asset is derecognised.
The Group assesses at each date of balance sheet whether a financial asset in form of trade receivables and unbilled receivables is impaired. In accordance with Ind AS
109, the Group applies Expected Credit Loss (ECL) model for measurement and recognition of impairment loss. As a practical expedient, the Group uses a provision
matrix to determine impairment loss on portfolio of its trade receivables. The provision matrix is based on available external and internal credit risk factors such as
credit default, age of receivables and Group’s historically observed default rates over the expected life of trade receivables and unbilled receivables. ECL impairment loss
allowance or reversal is recognised during the year as expense or income respectively in the restated statement of profit and loss.

settlement for atleast  twelve months after the reporting period, regardless of when the actual settlement is expected to occur.
Cancellation of ESOPs occurs only in cases where the options have not vested and the employee exits the organization. Unvested options automatically lapse upon

The cost of the defined benefit gratuity plan and other post-employment medical benefits and the present value of the gratuity obligation are determined using actuarial

sensitive to changes in these assumptions. All assumptions are reviewed at each reporting date.

Initial recognition and measurement 
Financial liabilities are classified, at initial recognition, as financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss. All financial liabilities are recognised initially at fair value
and, in the case of loans and borrowings and payables, net of directly attributable transaction costs.
The Group's financial liabilities include trade and other payables and borrowings
Financial assets at fair value through profit and loss ('FVTPL')
Financial assets in this category are those that are held for trading and have been either designated by management upon initial recognition or are mandatorily required
to be measured at fair value under Ind AS 109 i.e. they do not meet the criteria for classification as measured at amortised cost or FVOCI. The transaction costs directly
attributable to the acquisition of financial assets and liabilities at fair value through profit and loss are immediately recognised in Statement of Profit and Loss. Financial
assets at fair value through profit or loss are carried in the balance sheet at fair value with net changes in fair value recognised in the statement of profit and loss. 
Interest earned on instruments designated at FVTPL is accrued in interest income, using the EIR, taking into account any discount/ premium and qualifying transaction
costs being an integral part of instrument. Interest earned on assets mandatorily required to be measured at FVTPL is recorded using the contractual interest rate.
Dividend income on listed equity investments are recognised in the restated statement of profit and loss as other income when the right of payment has been
established.
Classification
The classification of financial assets at subsequent measurement depends on the financial asset’s contractual cash flow characteristics and the Group's business model
for managing them. With the exception of trade receivables that do not contain a significant financing component or for which the Group has applied the practical
expedient, the Group initially measures a financial asset at its fair value plus, in the case of a financial asset not at fair value through profit or loss, transaction costs.
Trade receivables that do not contain a significant financing component or for which the Group has applied the practical expedient are measured at the transaction price
determined under Ind AS 115.
In order for a financial asset to be classified and measured at amortised cost or fair value through OCI, it needs to give rise to cash flows that are ‘solely payments of
principal and interest (SPPI)’ on the principal amount outstanding. This assessment is referred to as the SPPI test and is performed at an instrument level. Financial
assets with cash flows that are not SPPI are classified and measured at fair value through profit or loss, irrespective of the business model.
The Group's business model for managing financial assets refers to how it manages its financial assets in order to generate cash flows. The business model determines
whether cash flows will result from collecting contractual cash flows, selling the financial assets, or both. Financial assets classified and measured at amortised cost are
held within a business model with the objective to hold financial assets in order to collect contractual cash flows while financial assets classified and measured at fair
value through OCI are held within a business model with the objective of both holding to collect contractual cash flows and selling.
Purchases or sales of financial assets that require delivery of assets within a time frame established by regulation or convention in the marketplace (regular way trades)
are recognised on the trade date, i.e., the date that the Group commits to purchase or sell the asset.
Financial assets at fair value through other comprehensive income ('FVOCI') (debt instruments)
Financial assets are measured at fair value through other comprehensive income if these financial assets are held within a business whose objective is achieved by both
collecting contractual cash flows and selling financial assets and the contractual terms of the financial asset give rise on specified dates to cash flows that are solely
payments of principal and interest on the principal amount outstanding. Debt instruments included within the FVTOCI category are measured initially as well as at each
reporting date at fair value. For debt instruments, at fair value through OCI, interest income, foreign exchange revaluation and impairment losses or reversals are
recognised in the profit or loss and computed in the same manner as for financial assets measured at amortised cost. The remaining fair value changes are recognised in
OCI. Upon derecognition, the cumulative fair value changes recognised in OCI is reclassified from the equity to profit or loss. 
De-recognition of financial assets
A financial asset (or, where applicable, a part of a financial asset or part of a group of similar financial assets) is primarily derecognised (i.e. removed from the Group's
balance sheet) when:
►	The rights to receive cash flows from the asset have expired, or
► The Group has transferred its rights to receive cash flows from the asset or has assumed an obligation to pay the received cash flows in full without material delay to a
third party under a ‘pass-through’ arrangement; and either (a) the Group has transferred substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset, or (b) the Group has neither
transferred nor retained substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset, but has transferred control of the asset.
When the Group has transferred its rights to receive cash flows from an asset or has entered into a pass-through arrangement, it evaluates if and to what extent it has
retained the risks and rewards of ownership. When it has neither transferred nor retained substantially all of the risks and rewards of the asset, nor transferred control
of the asset, the Group continues to recognise the transferred asset to the extent of the Group's continuing involvement. In that case, the Group also recognises an
associated liability. The transferred asset and the associated liability are measured on a basis that reflects the rights and obligations that the Group has retained.
Continuing involvement that takes the form of a guarantee over the transferred asset is measured at the lower of the original carrying amount of the asset and the
maximum amount of consideration that the Group could be required to repay.
Financial assets at amortised cost
Financial assets are subsequently measured at amortised cost if these financial assets are held within a business whose objective is to hold these assets in order to collect
contractual cash flows and the contractual terms of the financial asset give rise on specified dates to cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest on the
principal amount outstanding. 
After initial measurement, such financial assets are subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest rate (EIR) method and are subject to
impairment as per the accounting policy applicable to ‘Impairment of financial assets.’ Amortised cost is calculated by taking into account any discount or premium on
acquisition and fees or costs that are an integral part of the EIR. The EIR amortisation is included in other income in the profit or loss. The losses arising from impairment
are recognised in the profit or loss. The Group's financial assets at amortised cost includes trade receivables, and loan to a director included under other non-current
financial assets.
Fair value of financial instrument
In determining the fair value of its financial instrument, the Group uses the methods and assumptions based on market conditions and risk existing at each reporting
date. Methods of assessing fair value result in general approximation of value and such value may never actually be realized. For all other financial instrument, the
carrying amounts approximate the fair value due to short maturity of those instruments.
Subsequent measurement
For purposes of subsequent measurement, financial assets are classified in four categories:
►	Financial assets at amortised cost (debt instruments)
►	Financial assets at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVTOCI) with recycling of cumulative gains and losses (debt instruments)
►	Financial assets designated at fair value through OCI with no recycling of cumulative gains and losses upon derecognition (equity instruments) 
►	Financial assets at fair value through profit or loss

Contingent liability
Contingent liability is-
(a) a possible obligation arising from past events and whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of one or more uncertain future
events not wholly within the control of the entity, or 
(b)	a present obligation that arises from past events but is not recognized because

-	 the amount of the obligation cannot be measured with sufficient reliability.

any outflow in settlement is remote.

The Group is subject to Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) obligation in accordance with the Rules notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change (MoEFCC). Considering specific requirements of the applicable Rules, the Group recognises provision toward EPR obligation when the obligation arises as per the
Rules notified, viz, as products are sold in the market. Initial recognition is based on recycling target prescribed under the Rules and amount expected to be incurred at
the time of recycling. The initial estimate of obligation is revised annually.
The cost of the defined benefit gratuity plan and the present value of the gratuity obligation are determined using actuarial valuations. An actuarial valuation involves
making various assumptions that may differ from actual developments in the future. These include the determination of the discount rate, future salary increases
attrition rates and mortality rates. Due to the complexities involved in the valuation and its long-term nature, a defined benefit obligation is highly sensitive to changes in
these assumptions. All assumptions are reviewed at each reporting date.
The parameter most subject to change is the discount rate. In determining the appropriate discount rate, the management considers the interest rates of government
bonds in currencies consistent with the currencies of the post-employment benefit obligation.
The Group provides warranties for its products, undertaking to repair or replace the product that fail to perform satisfactory during the warranty period. Provision made 
at the year-end represents the amount of expected cost of meeting such obligations of rectification / replacement which is based on the historical warranty claim
information as well as recent trends that might suggest that past cost information may differ from future claims. Factors that could impact the estimated claim
information include the success of the Group’s productivity and quality initiatives. Provision towards warranty is disclosed in Note 19b.
Estimates are required to determine the appropriate discount rate used to measure lease liabilities. The Group cannot readily determine the interest rate implicit in the
lease, therefore, it uses its incremental borrowing rate (IBR) to measure lease liabilities. The IBR is the rate of interest that the Group would have to pay to borrow over a
similar term, and with a similar security, the funds necessary to obtain an asset of a similar value to the right-of-use asset in a similar economic environment. The IBR
therefore reflects what the Group ‘would have to pay’, which requires estimation when no observable rates are available or when they need to be adjusted to reflect the
terms and conditions of the lease. The Group estimates the IBR using observable inputs (such as market interest rates, bank rates to the Group for a loan of a similar
tenure, etc). The Group has applied a single discount rate to a portfolio of leases of similar assets in similar economic environment with a similar end date.
When the fair values of financial assets and financial liabilities recorded in the Restated Consolidated Summary Statement of Assets and Liabilities cannot be measured
based on quoted prices in active markets, their fair value is measured using appropriate valuation techniques. The inputs for these valuations are taken from observable
sources where possible, but where this is not feasible, a degree of judgement is required in establishing fair values. Judgements include considerations of various inputs
including liquidity risk, credit risk, volatility etc. Changes in assumptions/judgements about these factors could affect the reported fair value of financial instruments.
Refer Note 36 of restated consolidated summary statements for the fair value disclosures and related sensitivity.
The holding company initially measures the cost of cash-settled transactions with employees using a binomial model to determine the fair value of the liability incurred.
Estimating fair value for share-based payment transactions requires determination of the most appropriate valuation model, which is dependent on the terms and
conditions of the grant. This estimate also requires determination of the most appropriate inputs to the valuation model including the expected life of the share option,
volatility and dividend yield and making assumptions about them.
The impairment provisions for trade receivables disclosed are based on assumptions about risk of default and expected loss rates. The Company uses judgement in
making these assumptions and selecting the inputs to the impairment calculation, based on the Company’s provisioning policy, history, existing market conditions as
well as forward looking estimates at the end of each reporting period. Estimates and judgements are continually evaluated. They are based on historical experience
and other factors, including expectations of future events that may have a financial impact on the Company and that are believed to be reasonable under the
circumstances.
The Group applied for the first-time certain standards and amendments, which are effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025. The Group has not
early adopted any standard, interpretation or amendment that has been issued but is not yet effective.
(i) Amendments to Ind AS 21 - Lack of exchangeability
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) notified the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules, 2025, which amend Ind AS 21, The Effects of Changes
in Foreign Exchange Rates to specify how an entity should assess whether a currency is exchangeable and how it should determine a spot exchange rate when
exchangeability is lacking. The amendments also require disclosure of information that enables users of its financial statements to understand how the currency not
being exchangeable into the other currency affects, or is expected to affect, the entity’s financial performance, financial position and cash flows. 
The amendments are effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025. When applying the amendments, an entity cannot restate comparative
information. 
The amendments do not have a material impact on the Group’s financial statements.
(ii) Amendments to Ind AS 1 - Classification of Liabilities as Current or Non-current and Non-current Liabilities with Covenants
In August 2025, the MCA notified amendments to paragraphs 69 to 76 of Ind AS 1 to specify the requirements for classifying liabilities as current or non-current. The
amendments clarify: 
• What is meant by a right to defer settlement 
• That a right to defer must exist at the end of the reporting period 
• That classification is unaffected by the likelihood that an entity will exercise its deferral right 
• That only if an embedded derivative in a convertible liability is itself an equity instrument would the terms of a liability not impact its classification 
In addition, a requirement has been introduced to require disclosure when a liability arising from a loan agreement is classified as non-current and the entity’s right to
defer settlement is contingent on compliance with future covenants within twelve months. 
If there is a breach of a material covenant of a long term loan arrangement on or before the end of the reporting period, resulting in the liability becoming payable on
demand as at the reporting date, and the lender agrees—after the reporting period but before the financial statements are approved for issue, not to demand repayment
for at least 12 months as a consequence of the breach, this shall be treated as an adjusting event. Accordingly, the entity is not required to classify the liability as current.
The amendments are effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025 retrospectively in accordance with Ind AS 8.

In August 2025, the MCA notified amendments to Ind AS 12 Income Taxes in response to the OECD’s BEPS Pillar Two rules and include: 
•A mandatory temporary exception to the recognition and disclosure of deferred taxes arising from the jurisdictional implementation of the Pillar Two model rules; and 
•Disclosure requirements for affected entities to help users of the financial statements better understand an entity’s exposure to Pillar Two income taxes arising from
that legislation, particularly before its effective date. 
The mandatory temporary exception – the use of which is required to be disclosed – applies immediately. The remaining disclosure requirements apply for annual
reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025, but not for any interim periods ending on or before March 31, 2026. 
The amendments had no impact on the Group’s consolidated financial statements as the Group is not in scope of the Pillar Two model rules.

Retained earnings 
Retained earnings represent the cumulative net profits/losses of the group earned from the commencement of its operations up to the reporting date, after
deducting amounts transferred to other reserves, dividends declared and paid, and any other distributions made to shareholders. These earnings serve as an
internal source of finance and reflect the portion of profits/losses that has been reinvested in the business rather than distributed. 
Securities premium represents the amount received by the group over and above the face value of shares issued. This reserve arises when shares are issued at a
price higher than their nominal value and is credited to the Securities Premium Account in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
The utilisation of securities premium is restricted by law and can only be applied for specific purposes as prescribed under Section 52 of the Companies Act,
2013, including:
> Issuance of fully paid bonus shares to shareholders.
> Writing off preliminary expenses of the group.
> Writing off expenses, commission, or discount allowed on the issue of shares or debentures.
> Providing for the premium payable on redemption of any redeemable preference shares or debentures.
> Purchase of own shares or other securities under the buy-back provisions of the Act.
The ESOP Outstanding Reserve represents the equity component arising from the recognition of share-based payment expenses related to Employee Stock
Option Plans (ESOPs).
This fair value is then recognised as an employee compensation expense over the vesting period of the options, with a corresponding credit to the ESOP
Outstanding Reserve under the equity section of the balance sheet.
The key purpose of this reserve is to reflect the group’s obligation to issue shares in the future upon the exercise of vested options, without involving any
immediate cash outflow.
The amounts recognised in this reserve are transferred to Securities Premium when Options are exercised by the employees or they expire unexercised.
The Capital Redemption Reserve is a statutory reserve created in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 when a group buys back its own
shares or redeems preference shares out of its distributable profits.
The purpose of this reserve is to maintain the group’s capital base and protect the interests of creditors by ensuring that an amount equal to the nominal value of
the shares bought back or redeemed is retained within the group’s equity, even though the number of issued shares is reduced.
The Non-controlling Interest Reserve is a component of equity that represents the share of net assets in a subsidiary that belongs to shareholders other than the
holding company.
When group has a subsidiary whose functional currency is different from the reporting currency of the holding company, their financial statements need to be
translated into the reporting currency for consolidation purposes. During this translation process, differences arise due to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates
and the same is recognized in foreign currency translation reserve.
Other comprehensive income include re-measurement loss / (gain) on defined benefit plans, net of taxes that will not be reclassified to Statement of Profit and

On 21 November 2025, the Central Government issued four separate notifications in the Official Gazette announcing implementation of four Labour Codes, viz., the Code on Wages, 2019,
the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. These four codes replace and consolidate
29 existing labour laws. Following the implementation of the four labour codes, the Central Government has pre-published the draft rules on 31 December 2025 under the respective
Labour Codes, for public comment and the final rules are expected to be notified in due course. To ensure smooth implementation, the Ministry of Labour and Employment has also
issued the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the four codes.
The four codes prescribe an inclusive definition of the term ‘wages’, which among other matters is relevant for determination of post-employment benefits including gratuity to all
employees. In accordance with the definition, certain specified items forming part of remuneration are not included in the wages and these excluded items cannot exceed 50% of total
remuneration. If there is an excess, then it is presumed that excess amount also forms part of wages. The four codes also introduce changes related to leave entitlement and encashment
for workers. Going forward, workers’ leave balance in excess of 30 days will be encashed at the end of each calendar year and workers will have a right to demand encashment for entire
leave.
The Group has assessed the impact of these changes on the basis of legal view obtained by the and the best information available till approval of the financial statements for issue. The

Basic EPS amounts are calculated by dividing the profit/loss for the year attributable to equity holders of the holding company by the weighted average number of equity shares
outstanding during the year including equity shares that will be issued upon the conversion of mandatorily convertible instruments, i.e. Compulsory convertible preference shares and
compulsory convertible debentures. The agreed conversion ratio is 1:1 meaning 1 equity share will be issued against 1 preference share or 1 debenture and the same is factored in the
calculation of weighted average number of shares outstanding during the year.
Diluted EPS amounts are calculated by dividing the profit/loss attributable to equity holders of the holding company by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding
during the year plus the weighted average number of equity shares that would be issued on conversion of all the dilutive potential equity shares into equity shares.

The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated using a discount rate determined by reference to 
government bond yields; if the return on plan asset is below this rate, it will create a plan deficit. Currently the plan has a 
relatively balanced investment in Government securities and debt instruments.
A decrease in the bond interest rate will increase the plan liability; however, this will be partially offset by an increase in the 
value of the plan’s debt investments.
The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the best estimate of the mortality of plan 
participants both during and after their employment. An increase in the life expectancy of the plan participants will increase 
the plan’s liability.
The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the future salaries of plan participants. As 
such, an increase in the salary of the plan participants will increase the plan’s liability.

internal review structure, whereby the its Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM) now reviews the Group’s performance and allocates
resources into business segments based on its products and has three reportable segments. The management has restated the segment
information for the previous financial year ended March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024 in accordance with the reporting requirements of

ii) Kitchen appliances business which comprises of mixer grinder, cold press juicer and water purifier
iii) Proprietory components business which comprises of motors and others
The Group has identified CEO as Chief Operating Decision Maker (‘CODM’) who reviews and allocates resources based on above
mentioned “Business Segments”.
Revenue and expenses : Revenue and expenses are attributed to the segments based on the direct relationship to the specific activities of
each segment. This includes both directly attributable costs and revenue and a proportionate allocation of common cost to each segment.
Certain income (i.e. interest, gain on mutual fund, forex fluctuation and other income) and certain expenses (i.e. employee benefit
expenses and other expenses comprising of corporate and administrative expenses, depreciation, amortization, and finance cost) are not
specifically allocable to segments and accordingly these expenses are adjusted against the total revenue.
As per para 23 of IND AS 108 ‘Operating Segments’, an entity shall report a measure of total assets and liabilities for each reportable
segment if such amounts are regularly provided to CODM. Since the information relating to segment assets and segment liabilities are not
provided to or reviewed by CODM, they are not disclosed in accordance with IND AS.
